At least some of us ought to read this book, and all of us may have cause to be grateful for its publication. It is a collection of papers presenting in shortened form some of the research now being done into the possibility of having verifiable ideas about what goes on in the course of an analysis. We need verifiable, testable ideas that would persuade

420

even Sanskritologists, musicologists and cosmologists to reach the same conclusions as we do using the same definitions and methods. At present this is an unattainable ideal, and this book is about the problems that arise in pursuit of this ideal and how some of the problems may be overcome. The definitions, methods and conclusions presented here are often cumbersome, but they may be the foundations of something much more elegant - indeed, every now and again we catch a glimpse of it.

I would advise the reader of this book not to start with the first section ‘Research on the Process’ although it lays the foundation for all serious work and gives the reader an idea of just how difficult it is to establish even the basic categories in terms of which to think of our task and the ground rules for research of this kind. Readers may feel more encouraged to persevere if they start with the middle section, ‘Outcome Studies’. The first paper in this section is an overview of the University of Columbia Records Project, which has been kept going in one form or another for over 40 years. Among the interesting findings is that, taking nearly 300 analysands, 8 out of 10 who are judged ‘analysable’ at the start of their analysis were deemed to have received ‘maximum benefit’ when they finished, but rather less than half of them were deemed to have ‘developed an analytic process’ (become psychologically minded) by then. The definition of what it is to ‘develop an analytic process’ is interesting; a patient judged to have developed it would have been rated high on the following criteria:

They brought psychological data into the treatment because they recognized that it could be a source of understanding as well as of relief.

Both eyes were then blindfolded … Her hands were tied to the side of the bed… When she awoke her world had disappeared. She had no eyes. New pain tore at the places where they had been. She could not move her arms or hands. Mother had disappeared. Strange hands and voices assaulted her in unfamiliar routines. (p. 18)

This is the experence of 2-year-old ‘Lucy’ when she was hospitalized at 10 months for the correction of a squint. Characteristically, Carol Jeffrey reached beyond the referring agency's tags of ‘severe psychotic type’, ‘continual violent aggression’ and ‘mutism’ to the why place where Lucy's violence underpinned her valiant and lifeaffirming decision to survive.

Jeffrey's work with autistic children like Lucy is merely one example of the problems referred to in the subtitle. Through her 50 years as a psychotherapist, she frequently engaged in long, gruelling attempts to release pre-verbal and pre-birth experiences. At school, the staff secretly dubbed her ‘That Why Child’ because of the continual probing for ‘the search of the “why and what for” of experience’ that became the mainstay of her future career. She had boundless reserves of patience and learned to be amiably silent to avoid invading the barricaded world of the patient. Often she held her patients, not merely psychologically, but physically as in the case of a 15-year-old boy who attacked her with a jackknife. ‘My body reacted and I pressed myself right up against him and he dropped the knife and burst into tears’ (p. 1).

Science is often rewritten these days as the endless replay of knowledge driven by power. Anthropologist Allan Young's book is no exception. Its title is taken from an earlier researcher's account of ‘the harmony of illusions’ which results when scientists force their data to conform with their ‘personal will’. Young does much the same for the history of post-traumatic stress (PTSD).

He begins with the forced biological connection made by British surgeon John Erichsen in his 1866 account of ‘nervous shock’ following railway accidents, a diagnosis impelled by victims' claims for compensation. Young then recounts the forces leading to the World War I diagnosis of ‘shell shock’. He dwells particularly on W.H.R. Rivers's work. Like others, Rivers tended to diagnose shell shock in men from the ranks as due to congenital or acquired weakness of the will, but in officers as due to excessive will-power and emotional repression inculcated by their public school training ‘to meet without manifestation of fear any occasion likely to call forth this emotion’ (p. 65). Rivers accordingly urged that, in treating officers, doctors should pit their will against that of the patient:

We should lead the patient resolutely to face the situation provided by his painful experience.

We should point out to him that such experience… can never be thrust wholly out of his life …

His experience should be talked over in all its bearings. (Rivers, quoted by Young, p. 67)

Just as Yealland, as recounted by Pat Barker in her novel Regeneration, used electric shock to force his patients to talk, Rivers, says Young, used suggestion to the same end.

Europe and the Efpp: An Update

Brian Martindale

Brian Martindale

63 Lancaster Road, London W11 1QG

Brian Martindale  

This communication is an update on the European Federation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in the Public Sector (EFPP). The content is a sequel and supplement to the information given in the British Journal of Psychotherapy (8(1):824) in 1991. That earlier article described the background to the formation of the EFPP and gave an outline of its structure and objectives.

Membership

Membership of the EFPP remains through national networks of organizations of psychoanalytic psychotherapists in the European Community and European Free Trade Area. Each country may have either linked or independent networks of organizations representing three sections - adult psychoanalytic psychotherapy, child psychoanalytic psychotherapy and group psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Through these networks we have a membership now of about 10,000 professionals. Our high standards of training for the three sections have been a most helpful boundary, achieved in all cases by members of some national networks and accepted as a goal for other member countries in which public sector psychoanalytic psychotherapy is poorly developed. Though our focus remains on the development of services within the public sector, this is a less well defined concept in some Continental countries, but our overall thinking is that full membership of a component organization would imply capacity to function as a recognized practitioner or training organization for any public or third party system.

With these shared objectives and training standards, there have been substantial developments in a number of countries. Perhaps the most important has been the coming together for the first time of organizations from different cities in our member countries into a national network, with the long-term possibility of influencing professional development at that level and also giving a greater chance of influencing any legislative issues. The most striking example of this has been the formation of the Italian network with 600 members from seven organizations. In Spain, the major centres in Barcelona and Madrid have been working together and have carefully created a structure that will facilitate development and representation in all regions. A new introductory training programme has developed from nothing in an area involving Luxembourg and parts of Belgium and France. New journals are appearing in these regions.

James Fisher

Tavistock Marital Studies Institute, London

James Fisher  

Reviewing this book poses a number of difficult issues for a psychotherapist like myself who is committed both to psychoanalytic therapy with couples and to the values associated with a feminist, egalitarian framework. These are issues which we as psychotherapists of any persuasion avoid at the cost of our integrity, issues concerned with the values inherent in our discipline.

Dr Claire Rabin, a university social work lecturer in family and couple therapy and a therapist herself in Tel Aviv, draws on her research and therapy with couples in the USA, the UK and Israel. She has written a valuable and exhaustive survey of a therapeutic approach to couples grounded in what contemporary sociologists describe as the values of the ‘companionate marriage’- or to use the term Dr Rabin cites, ‘peer marriages’. This is clear in the expressive title she has chosen, emphasizing both the twin goals of equality and friendship in marriage and the task of the therapist as ‘empowering’. One important strength of the book is the extensive use of the sociological and ‘family and marital therapy’ literature concerning both contemporary aspirations towards equality and friendship in intimate relationships and the correlation between sexist patterns and marital distress. If for no other reason, the book is worth reading for bringing the reader up-to-date on a literature which psychoanalytic psychotherapists all too often ignore.

A second strength of Dr Rabin's book is her inclusion of detailed clinical illustrations, along with extensive quotations from research couples, which allow the reader to see clearly how she uses her principles of an ‘empowering’ approach in the consulting-room. The spontaneous and conversational quality of the clinical examples derives from the fact that they are actual transcripts of recordings of sessions. It allows readers to form their own judgements of this way of working with couples. Dr Rabin acknowledges that this approach ‘shares a great deal with a sociological orientation to the family’, and I do not think it would be stretching the point, to use the term ‘socio-therapy’ rather than ‘psychotherapy’ to describe it. It is based originally on extensive interviewing of what she describes as ‘equal partner couples who were attempting to live a non-sexist lifestyle’. Not surprisingly (since we all tend to find what we are looking for), Dr Rabin also finds that the clinical couples she sees are uniformly troubled by overt or residual sexist assumptions and patterns of relating, whether or not they have explicitly egalitarian aspirations for their relationships.

George Craig  

To any but the most besotted admirer of the correspondents, this second volume must come, initially at least, as a disappointment. It is not just the drop in excitement that goes, perhaps inevitably, with familiarity-the two men know each other pretty well by now, while we as readers of the earlier volume have been able to follow the unfolding of their friendship-but something altogether simpler and more brutal: the Great War. As the dates show, almost all the letters are written in the shadow of the conflict between the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary and their few allies) and the largely Western alliance led by Britain, France and, later, the United States. And, of course, the Armistice of November 1918 brought scant comfort to the defeated. Throughout, Freud is tormented by worries about his family and, above all, his soldier sons; Ferenczi (serving as a Medical Officer) is caught up in endless schemes and negotiations for a better posting while continually confronting, in his work, the dreadful physical and psychic consequences of warfare; and both men are continually preoccupied by shortages, enforced separations, restrictions on travel, censorship, and all the paraphernalia of world war. Much of what they write to each other could have been written by any two educated men of their time and place, while the things that are peculiar to them are also coloured by the war. Freud repeatedly laments his inability to write anything important or new, is gloomy about the future (even the present) of psychoanalysis, and has health worries. Ferenczi, always given to somatizing inner conflict, has enough symptoms to fill a textbook, and writes in detail about them all, while also deploring the drying up of his creativity. Both men badly miss the regular gatherings and congresses of the prewar years, and have to worry about whether they can get a reliable publisher, or even enough paper to make publication possible. Both are aware too of the rising tide of antisemitism.

Vico in the Consulting Room

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

Dear Editor

I was delighted to read Donald Phillip Verene's article, ‘Freud's Consulting Room Archaeology and Vico's Principles of Humanity: A Communication’, in the BJP 13(4), in which he considered some of the intellectual connections between these two original thinkers. I hope that what I add is taken in the spirit in which I intend, namely enthusiasm.

Vico is part of my thinking, and his links with Freud find their expression within my consulting room. In 1728 Vico wrote his Autobiography, and what was revolutionary and original about this work was that he believed that the history of ideas was to be found in the development of the ideas of an individual. He demonstrated his theory of mind in the very writing of his Autobiography. In the consulting room I believe that one of the tasks is to find a way in which the individual can come to know his or her own mind through writing (figuratively) their autobiography. If an individual can come to understand how their beliefs have come about, and trace the development of these beliefs, then something else happens within the mind. Vico was the first Western philosopher to distinguish between two concepts of knowing, which he called the ‘verum-factum’ principle. Put very simply, he suggested that the only knowledge that we could claim to be ‘true’ was to be found within the mind of man. ‘The rule and criterion of truth is to have made it. We can know nothing that we have not made.’ He then went on to say that we do not have such criteria for our knowledge of the natural world for that has been created by God. Now where Vico's ‘verum-factum’ principle impinges upon what happens in the consulting room is that, as the individual ‘writes’ his psycho-biography, the individual indeed comes to know that what is within his or her own mind is self-created. At that moment the terrifying fantasies become part of the creative imagination.

I believe that Vico's theory of mind is truly revolutionary, and moreover that he is one of the forefathers of psychoanalytic thinking. Freud may not have read Vico's New Science nor his Autobiography but, in their different ways, Freud and Vico both came to know that a Theory of Mind can only take place within the mind of man.

Lydia Tischler

Lydia Tischler  

This is a most welcome addition to the meagre literature on countertransference in psychoanalytic psychotherapy and psychoanalysis with children and adolescents which, whatever the preferred definition, has become an indispensable technical tool

567

for the majority of child psychotherapists. It is especially welcome as a first, in what promises to be an important series of clinical monographs on subjects relevant to psychotherapists working in the public sector, bringing together the views and experiences of practitioners from a number of European countries and working in diverse settings. Furthermore it is to be applauded as an enterprise in cooperation between member countries representing child and adolescent, individual adult and group psychotherapists.

In the Introduction Tsiantis outlines the main themes of each chapter written by the various authors: Anastasopoulos and Tsiantis, Judith Trowell, Alex Holder, Anne-Marie Sandler, François Ladame, Jacqueline Godfrind, Anne Alvarez, Didier Houzel, and John Tsiantis. The authors' differences in practice and technique, states Tsiantis, are underpinned by ‘a unified body of psychoanalytic thought’ (p. 16). The reader will find this chapter useful as a guide to the rest of the monograph.

In Chapter 1, Anastasopoulos and Tsiantis give a brief history of the development of the concept, beginning with Freud and followed by a selected review of the literature on countertransference with special reference to work with children and adolescents. They write about the relationship between countertransference and projective identification and finally conduct a more detailed discussion of factors likely to evoke countertransference reactions, and the interrelationship between them as they relate to the child, to the adolescent, to those stemming from parents and families and from the therapist herself.'

The review provides a fine balance of the definitions of countertransference from the extreme ‘totalistic’ to the ‘classicist’ view, and shades in between. The former, represented by such authors as Kohut, Little and Shane, regards countertransference to be ‘the total response of the child analyst to the patient, the parents and the therapeutic situation’ while the classicist view is espoused by Ladame who, tongue in cheek, defines countertransference as a rationalization for the analyst contemplating her navel. The more prevalent view, however, summarized by Epstein and Feiner regards countertransference as the contribution which the therapist makes to the therapeutic process.

The Origins of Disquieting Discoveries by Melanie Klein: The Possible Significance of the Case of ‘Erna’

Claudia Frank and Heinz Weib

Using the example of the analysis of 6-year-old Erna, which extended over more than two years and was the longest treatment conducted by Melanie Klein in her Berlin years, the authors demonstrate the importance of her early child analyses for the development of some of her concepts and hence for a decisive advance in psychoanalysis itself. For this purpose they adduce unpublished original documents found among Klein's papers in London, which include autobiographical material, the text of her Wurzburg lecture on her obsessional-neurotic little patient, handwritten session notes, and drawings by Erna herself. Although in the authors' view Klein attempted to accommodate her findings within Freud's theoretical framework, her clinical experience of the psychic reality of the relational world of early oedipality eventually called for the introduction of new concepts. The combined parent figure, primary sadism, the paranoidschizoid position, splitting, the relevance of the death drive to the superego, and later formulations on reparation, envy and gratitude are all shown to be foreshadowed in Klein's account of the treatment of Erna. After some retrospective considerations of Erna's analysis and a fleeting glimpse of Erna as an adult, the authors conclude by emphasizing the significance of Klein's emigration to England for the subsequent flowering of her work.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis77, 1213, 1996

How Useful is Selection?

Willem Kappelle

The author begins by reviewing the literature on the selection of applicants for psychoanalytic training. Having himself been active in a training role in the Dutch Society for many years, he then discusses that society's selection approach and compares it with the literature reports, which he in many cases finds inconclusive and incomplete, partly because relevant information is often unavailable for reasons of discretion. A major problem is stated to be the difficulty of defining the concept of a good psychoanalyst. Although most of the published material concentrates on the qualities of the applicant, it is pointed out that the selectors and the manner of their interaction with the applicant are also important. The centrepiece of the paper is a detailed report on the results of a survey by the author of the methods used by the Dutch Society's selectors over a 17-year period, in which the approaches of selectors of different ages and backgrounds and their responses to different types of applicants are compared by statistical techniques. Selection methods proved to be largely intuitive and the survey respondents had difficulty in defining the criteria they used. For all the imponderables, the author notes that no training committee is prepared to abandon selection-usually by interview-even if it can ultimately do no more than assess an applicant's analysability and life accomplishments.

Clive Eiles

Clive Eiles

Clive Eiles  

I must risk annoying the reader: this is the second of a pair of books which need to be thought of as one. The first, also published in 1996, is called The Broad-Spectrum Psychotherapist (Bramley 1996), and the two were clearly planned, and perhaps written, as a pair.

Wyn Bramley also risks annoying at least this reader by putting in each title an expression, ‘Broad-Spectrum Psychotherapy’, that initially has a meaning for her alone. The premise behind the expression is that five times a week psychoanalysis without time limit, with selected patients, is important and valuable. It is, however, sometimes thought of as the paradigm, the best, against which other kinds of psychologically based treatments are measured; and when we carry out one of these we often tend to think that what we are doing is second or third best.

More is taken to mean better and less to mean worse. At the end of this chain is the therapist, often working in the public sector, where the amount of time available for any patient is limited often to one session a week for a duration which is also measured in weeks. Many therapists also work in GP practices where the work is time limited, with the range of patients and the problems they bring very broad. Not only this, but the patients are not closely selected for suitability. If you do this kind of work the patients you get to work with are those who walk through the door, and one part of the challenge is to find, and to find quickly, something valid which can be done in the short time available.

I should declare my interest in that I work in a GP practice and meet regularly with a group of colleagues. A short while ago we put together a paper which we sent to the local Health Commission, which contained a number of clinical vignettes, intended to illustrate the range of patients we see, who include the borderline and the psychotic. The work we described ranged between contributing to patient management and extended assessment. If psychoanalysis is high-tech surgery, brief work in a GP practice is MASH.

I am a psychodynamically-trained counsellor. The following case is from counselling work in a Family Service Unit. All my work with parents and infants is supervised by experienced child psychotherapists who specialize in parent-infant work.

Lydia was referred to see me at the Family Service Unit by another counsellor who was seeing her son Jay, aged 7 years, once weekly for depression.

Lydia's extremely haggard, depressed appearance had aroused alarm in all the staff who entered the Unit's waiting-room. Various concerned staff members approached her as she sat tearfully waiting while Jay had his session. Lydia asked to see a counsellor. Jay's counsellor made an appointment with me for the following week. The counsellor told me that the family were black British, that Lydia's parents were born in Jamaica. Anthony Bateman  

A creative and constructive partnership between different psychotherapies needs to develop if a psychotherapeutic psychiatry is to flourish. The greatest threat to the development of psychotherapeutic psychiatry is the partisan approach of the psychotherapies themselves. Prejudicial attitudes prevent acquisition of useful knowledge and its appropriate assimilation in psychiatric settings. The concepts of the self and borderline personality are used to show how understanding different psychotherapeutic approaches can inform treatment and further the development of a fruitful psychotherapeutic psychiatry which is itself essential for the treatment of severe personality disorder.

Meg Williams

Meg Williams

The Bourne, Redlands Lane, Crondall, Farnham, Surrey GU10 5RF

Meg Williams  

The intention of this paper is to focus attention on the nature and value of inspiration as a function of particular importance in all aesthetic work, including psychoanalysis; and to indicate its analogous importance in personality development. Following the poets - the most expressive analysts of inspiration - inspiration is described as a mental process rather than a quality. This paper does not rely solely on mere statements about inspiration. Rather, features of the concept of inspiration are drawn from the aesthetic language of several poets: in particular, Dante, Keats, Milton, Emily Bronte, Plato. Finally, some more explicit links are made to the context of current psychoanalytic theory.

Ethical Moments in Psychotherapy: Interpretation, Seduction or …?

Miles Clapham

Miles Clapham

Chevening Road, Greenwich, London SE10 0LB

Miles Clapham  

Following Wittgenstein's consideration of ethics, the term ‘ethical moments’ describes certain moments in psychotherapy that seem not to be able to be captured in language, although language expresses something in the moment. Wittgenstein has said that the basis of ethics, and indeed of philosophy, cannot be put into either logical or empirical propositions. Expressions that arise out of ‘the existence of language’ show rather a poetic response in these moments that are felt to be profound. These expressions can be shown to be neither factual nor logical, yet nevertheless ‘hit the mark’.

Moments in psychotherapeutic practice are used to illustrate this clinically, and the nature of interpretation at these times is considered both in relation to Wittgenstein's discussion of the limits of logic and of language, and to the psychoanalytic view that not to interpret is to be seduced by the patient. It is held that in these ethical moments something transpires beyond the reach of theory-based interpretation.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The existence of an unconscious mind connecting us to the rest of the world and to our fellow beings, that is both basically reality-orientated and phantasy-prone, that possesses both innate wisdom and folly, composed of and related to the past, present and future, is a founding doctrine of the psychoanalytic view. Moreover, the dynamic unconscious is in constant motion, forming and dissolving patterns, providing us, when we can gain a momentary glimpse, with therapeutic opportunities. Unconscious truth speaks to us indirectly, often in the gaps and slips surrounding rational speech. In the first paper in this issue, a slip is made by a young woman in speaking to her father and the authors, Judy Tame Wall and Del Loewenthal, analyse its meaning according to three contrasting theories, those of Freud, Laing and Lacan. This Journal has a long-held interest in comparative studies, believing that they foster thinking.

Comparisons often lead to integrative theories. The second paper by Paul March is a study of psychotherapy that employs an amalgam of cognitive-behavioural and psychoanalytic techniques. When patients don't do their homework, a psychotic sub-personality is hypothesized, morose, uncooperative and unable to learn, which takes over the functioning of the person.

Next, Patricia Polledri reports on the psychotherapy with a man who murdered his mother as an adolescent, perceiving her as an agent of evil. Intrapsychic changes occurred as a result of psychoanalytically-based psychotherapy in a Secure Unit. Patrick Gallwey supplies the Foreword to this paper, setting out the background to forensic psychotherapy, the treatment of patients who exhibit dangerous behaviour or who are criminally ill.

Following this, Anthony Bateman uses the term ‘psychotherapeutic psychiatry’ to describe the integration of cognitive, psychodynamic and biological approaches in the treatment of severely disturbed borderline patients, arguing for a creative partnership between the psychotherapies if we are all to flourish. The partisan approach of the psychotherapies, indeed their oppositional stances, their quarrelling and devaluation of one another, compromises patient care and holds back our development, obscuring our aims in fruitless struggles for political supremacy.

International Journal of Psycho Analysis77, 871, 1996

Multi-Lingualism, Word-Presentations, Thing-Presentations and Psychic Reality

Juan Eduardo Tesone

The author begins by noting that psychoanalysts have concerned themselves with the relationship between language and thought ever since Freud published On Aphasia in 1891 but that surprisingly little attention has been paid to multi-lingualism in the analytic situation. He contends that the use of a foreign language may act as a detour with the aim of gaining distance from the mother's voice, thereby avoiding emotional and instinctual overload. Some clinical vignettes are presented, involving the case of an Italian patient having analysis in French with an Argentinian analyst of Italian origin living in France. Italian words and phrases that occasionally come up are the vehicle for oedipal feelings and archaic representations, and the analyst's knowledge of Italian language and culture allows him to turn the relevant associations to account in the analysis. The use of a foreign language is stated to perform a similar function to negation, permitting an oracular type of ambiguity that protects the patient from the failure of repression and breakdown of the protective shield against stimuli. Following a note on the Pirandellian nature of the affective representation of the drive, the author ends with some considerations on the relations between word-presentations and thing-presentations and on how these might be modified in the foreign-language situation.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis77, 1996

Thirty Methods to Destroy the Creativity of Psychoanalytic Candidates

Otto F. Kernberg

The author explores formal aspects of psychoanalytic education relevant to the fostering or inhibiting of creativity in the work of candidates. He refers to 30 features of psychoanalytic institutes that inhibit candidates' -creativity and, by implication, illustrate problems in psychoanalytic education that require our attention. These features include systematic slowing down of institutional progression of candidates, repetitive and unquestioning teaching of key papers by Freud, monolithic tendencies regarding theoretical approaches, isolation of candidates from the professional and scientific activities of the psychoanalytic society, accentuation of the hieratical relations among the psychoanalytic faculty, graduation rituals, discouragement of original contributions by candidates, intellectual isolation of institutes, lack of full presentation of clinical work by senior members of the faculty, neglect of studies of controversies regarding psychoanalytic technique, ‘paranoiagenic’ features of the relationship among faculty and regarding requirements for candidates, the ‘convoy’ system, neglect of exploration of the scientific and cultural boundaries and applications of psychoanalysis and the effects of institutional conflicts around the appointment of training analysts.

Clinical Commentary XXI

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold  

The material presented for comment is a piece of parent-infant work, which gives a chance to consider a new and expanding area of clinical specialism which is claimed to enable new populations to benefit from psychoanalytic thinking (Stern 1995). The richness of the material brought to such work seems to derive from two aspects of the impact of parenting upon the individual. One is a strong wish to provide the best possible care for the child, which enables approaches to be made to areas of the self which would usually remain out of reach of psychic intervention. This has been clearly seen for many years by workers in child and family psychiatric clinics. The other related fact is that immediately the parent brings the juxtaposition of their own experiences as a child in the past and in memory, interacting with their own parents, the child they are parenting themselves in outside reality, and their wishes, fears and phantasies for the future for themselves and their infant. The enormously valuable role of infant observation emerges clearly in this piece, enabling us to experience the intense feelings generated by close contact with infants (Rustin 1989).

Recently the Association for Infant Mental Health-UK has been formed to provide a forum for discussion and contact between the different professions working together in the field. The Hon. Sec. is Asha Phillips AIMH-UK, The Tavistock Centre, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA.

Commentary by a Child and Adult Psychotherapist

Stella Acquarone

Stella Acquarone

27B Frognal, London NW3 6AR

Stella Acquarone  

When reading this clinical material, six areas of inquiry spring to mind: (1) the mother (apart from the others), (2) the baby as individual, (3) the counsellor as observer and stimulus, (4) the mother/counsellor dynamic, (5) the session events, and (6) the context of the behaviour observed.

The overall outcomes in this material - as applied to the six areas above - spring from my contention that the behaviours of the participants in this material are centred in root causes: (1) the mother acts from her own child-identity, (2) the baby ‘fights’, she fights her mother's passivity, the conditions of her own birth, and for the things missing in her own development, and (3) the counsellor identifies with the mother, perhaps prematurely.

These external objects and root causes make up the premises. How do we arrive at psychotherapeutic conclusions? We look at internal objects.

Northern Exposure

Don Feasey

Don Feasey

Don Feasey  

Dear Editor

I write to congratulate you for including the article ‘The Abuse of Power Within the Analytic Setting’ by Marguerite Valentine in the Winter issue of the BJP. It seems to me it is high time a somewhat censored subject received a public hearing and, hopefully, discussion within the training bodies that currently exist, not only for training psychoanalysts from the traditional schools of thought, but also those currently working under the auspices of the UKCP training arrangements.

Most of the latter inherit the culture of psychoanalytic training and enjoy not only its benefits but also those practices and beliefs that have become, to quote Valentine, ‘reified’. And so what was once merely an idea or proposition to be examined and ‘played’ with becomes promoted as a fact. We have all felt our hearts sink when, in discussion or in personal therapy, we hear the authoritarian voice of analysis telling us that a suggestion, or metaphor, such as the ‘bad breast’, ‘good breast’ or the ‘unconscious’ becomes thrust upon us as essential objective experience with predetermined outcomes.

My special interest at present is in the issue of training supervision where much that is described by Valentine as occurring in personal therapy may be experienced in the training process. My views are elaborated in the Spring issue of the Journal of the West Midlands Institute for Psychotherapy. The splitting that has occurred in the training of psychoanalysts in London, which has given rise to such obsessively tight control of the supervision of trainees, is, I fear, being repeated by the newer bodies entering the field of training analytic psychotherapists. Some years ago I was advocating at the West Midlands Institute that we should offer a core course of teaching and learning covering the main schools of psychoanalytic thought, in a historical perspective, leading on to personal options chosen by trainees from within the structure of training. Trainees would then choose, in association with their options, appropriate personal therapists and supervisors - the latter being recognized by virtue of registration in the appropriate section of the UKCP and being in good measure independent of the training bodies. My aim was to try to ensure that trainees should remain together as a coherent body of persons sharing a training culture that was neither exclusive nor over controlling. My hope was that a dialogue would be set up within the trainee's experience of learning that would lead to a more open, democratic and less defensive atmosphere of professional training. This has not come about. The West Midlands Institute now has three training committees supervising discrete courses. In my opinion an opportunity was lost, the Institute ‘regressed’.

My immediate reaction to this stimulating collection of essays was to feel that the reader was being given generous access to the workings of the very active mind of a man at the mid-point of his life, both professional and personal. Having reasons to reflect back at the moment of changing course, he reproduces 16 different pieces of work between which there is a multiplicity of threads and associations which could even be described as ‘mind blowing’ for the unsuspecting enquirer. They range from earlier accounts of psychiatric and group-related topics through psychoanalysis, philosophy and political ideas, finding a common medium of expression as the book progresses in literature and especially poetry (see chapter 15, ‘Dark corners on poetry and melancholy’). This concludes, quoting Jeremy Reed: ‘It is what happens in the dark corners, in the hours when one is unrestrainably alone, that compromises the record of one's life.’ Wilson says, ‘Sylvia Plath has left us a graphic account of those dark places’ (p. 123).

The book is the second in a new series called Forensic Focus edited by Murray Cox. This series is appearing at a specific moment in time, recording the development of a new hybrid profession, forensic psychotherapy, mentioned by Murray Cox in the foreword and the specific subject of the other books in the series so far, at once exciting, complex and controversial. Sandwiched between a substantial textbook and a practical clinical guide, this contribution is on the one hand charming and informative and, on the other, idiosyncratic and anecdotal.

The Bereavement Game and the Divorced and Separated Game. Produced by Jessica Kingsley Publishers, 1996; £38.18.

Una Freeston and Jane Marsh

Jane Marsh

Broadstairs, Kent

Jane Marsh  

Each of these two games consists of a board on which is depicted a ‘journey’ connected respectively with bereavement or with divorce or separation. Counters are moved according to throws of the dice and certain squares contain instructions which directly or indirectly lead the child to a question relevant to the subject of the game.

The clinic to which the games were offered has, like similar clinics, been under heavy pressure from rising referrals, and the majority of the 800+ families referred last year had experienced divorce, separation or bereavement. It was therefore a puzzle to find that so few staff wanted to use the game. Two main reasons were given for this lack of uptake. In the first place, children are not referred on account of these experiences, but because the referrer cannot understand the connection between the known experience and the behaviour or the emotion of the child. Usually something else is also occurring, such as sexual abuse or parental inadequacy. The staff member needs a sophisticated understanding of all the relevant factors and sometimes felt that it was an artificial simplification to deal solely with a known fact. In addition, some people felt that the use of something called a ‘game’ trivialized misery. A game has other inherent connotations, all of which appeared when various children played the games.

A game is played with other people. When the games were used with individual children a staff member also had to play and to answer the questions in the light of experience. One staff member used her own bereavement and was disconcerted to find herself becoming unduly angry at one of the questions. This helped her to understand the child better and also to understand herself, but highlights the need for supervision, or at least debriefing for staff. The child in question benefited, saying, ‘I never knew other people felt that way too.’ A game is often relaxing. There was one boy whose parents had separated some years ago and the game revealed that the separation was not his major problem at the current time.

Introductory Remarks

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

18 Spencer Road, London SW18 2SW

Prophecy Coles  

On 26 April 1997 the Lincoln Centre put on its first public conference. It took place in the Montague Chambers of Southwark Cathedral in London. It was a half-day meeting, and there were two speakers: Dr Felicity de Zulueta, whose paper was called ‘Demonology versus Science?’, and Dr Christoph Hering, who spoke on ‘Beyond Understanding? Some Thoughts on the Meaning and Function of the Notion of “Evil”’. The subject of the conference had been suggested by Christoph Hering, when he was still living in England and working for the Lincoln Centre. He believed that psychoanalytic thinking had an important part to play in our understanding of some of the recent violent events against people that we had all been witness to, in the press and on TV - the massacre of schoolchildren at Dunblane, the murder of children by Fred and Rosemary West, to name but two. It seemed appropriate that a year after the Dunblane massacre the Lincoln Centre should come together and try and think about the issues that this event raised, and it seemed fitting that we should come together within the sanctity and safety of Southwark Cathedral. Indeed the quiet seriousness of the Cathedral and its space helped to contain the anxieties that the subject of the conference aroused.

The conference was sold out and it became apparent that the subject was addressing a public need, for people came from a wide range of backgrounds. As a result of the diversity of people's interests there was a richness to the questions and to the exchange, and some creative and healing thinking took place.

The conference was fortunate to have two independent-minded speakers, whose views offered all those present a wide-angled view on the subject. Their differing models of the mind enriched rather than polarized the thinking of everyone. Felicity de Zulueta gave a beautifully argued and researched paper, full of passion and conviction, on Attachment Theory and the links between damaged attachment and human violence. She expressed some disquiet at having been asked to speak at a conference that had such a title. She did not think that the concept of ‘evil’ was a useful one to apply to human violence, for it implied the moral superiority of those who used it and did nothing to help us to understand and to try to resolve why humans resort to violence. She spoke of the research that shows a strong correlation between the effects of broken attachment bonds, psychological stress and human destructiveness. If children are insecurely attached they become ‘avoidant’ or ‘disorganized’, and hostile and aggressive. This behaviour is a response to psychological trauma. The people who fill our prisons and our mental hospitals are these insecurely attached children. They are not ‘evil’ people; they are suffering and have been damaged by the failure of attachment. We need to help them, not to punish them further by labelling them as ‘evil’.

Commentary by an Anna Freud Centre Child Psychotherapist

Susan Yabsley

Susan Yabsley

21 Maresfield Gardens, London NW3 5SH

Susan Yabsley  

Responding to clinical material is always a difficult and challenging task. The written record of what has taken place in the therapeutic session can never entirely capture the subtleties of the clinical work. So much is unknown and unknowable to the reader and this, of course, gives rise to many questions and fantasies that may or may not prove useful. What follows is an attempt to organize some thoughts and questions that arose as I read the clinical material.

Our introduction to this case immediately plunges us into a profound state of concern. One of the first things we are told is that Lydia's extremely haggard and depressed appearance has aroused alarm in all the staff who enter the Family Service Unit's waiting-room. Her distress is such that it is spilling over into the waiting-room where her son, Jay, receives help and care. Jay has been seen at the centre once weekly for depression and, although we do not know how long they have been attending the clinic, the implication is that this reaction to Lydia is recent. What is it that is causing such alarm in the staff to the extent that various staff members approach her while her son is having his session, I wondered? It is within this atmosphere of anxiety and uncertainty that the counsellor has her initial meeting with Lydia. Unfortunately, the information gathered and the counsellor's observations during this meeting do not allay any of the initial concerns. We learn more about Lydia's and Dinitra's backgrounds that lead us to think their situation has been one of ongoing disturbance/ distress. For example, Lydia has been very depressed since Dinitra's birth and she is separated from her baby's father. Lydia has also had numerous medically unexplained black-outs. We also learn that she has been seeing a psychiatrist who has been making home visits since Dinitra's birth. The feelings of alarm that have arisen seem to be confirmed and the case must continue to be viewed as a severe one.

It seemed as if Lydia had reached a crisis point and was communicating this to the staff at the Family Service Unit. What had happened at this particular point in time? What were the triggers for Lydia's haggard appearance and for her request to see a counsellor? The psychiatrist informed the counsellor that he was completing work with Lydia that week, although he remained uncertain as to the nature of her problems.

From Oedipus to Dream by Mauro Mancia. Published by Karnac Books, London, 1996; 174 pages; £16.95

David Mann

David Mann

David Mann  

This is an interesting book by the Italian analyst Mauro Mancia. The chapters are based on seminars held in recent years. This does pose a slight problem in that the book does not have a clear focus or topic that is elaborated. In that sense it reads more like a collection of papers, whereas the title From Oedipus To Dream promises more continuity than is in fact present. The subjects range broadly, with chapters on the Oedipus complex, models and origins of the mind, the place of phantasy, the absent father, psychosomatic disorders and dreams. There is probably something of interest for just about everybody.

Though working as a post-Kleinian, Mancia has a critical appreciation of his theoretical tradition. In particular, he argues against the continued use of doubtful ideas, especially of the death instinct, for which there is no clinical proof that is not open to other interpretations. He argues instead that children vary in their innate emotional equipment to face frustrations. Therefore, they are not all equally capable of transforming the same amount of frustration. Thus concepts like ‘malignant narcissism’ are viewed as secondary to the disappointment with the object. I think that with a view such as this, Mancia is closer to the ideas of Fairbairn than Klein. He also cautions against isomorphism (pp. 34 and 63), that is the drawing of too close a parallel between mother-baby and analyst-patient relations, though clearly there is an analogy.

Mancia also advocates a more interactive mother and baby model with less emphasis simply on the infant's instincts and internal world. Citing Andre Green he writes, ‘the object is the revealing agent of the instinct. Without instincts the object is lifeless’ (p. 32). In that sense, the infant's innate psychic equipment explains the wide variables in how infants cope with reality. Desire is the pleasure-seeking part that enlivens the object. In this model, Mancia suggests that unconscious phantasy is not a primary formation but a secondary product derived from the complex process of adaptation originating from the meeting of instincts (wishes and needs) with the object. The author writes, ‘the fate of the human mind may well be played out in this gap between the wish and its fulfilment’ (p. 53).

In discussing these two books together, one theme which seemed to emerge for us was the importance of a therapeutic space that can be experienced as a safe place in which conflicts may be registered and worked through. Ilany Kogan describes how it can be created in an analytic setting. In work with survivors of the Holocaust, the space is always connected with imagery of death: its most important quality is that it affirms life in the shadow of death. The continuous presence of what Robert Jay Lifton (1968) calls the ‘death imprints’ of the original ordeal correspondingly marks the lives of the second generation. Anne Karpf's book illustrates these themes in many ways.

Brendan McLoughlin

Brendan McLoughlin

Bath

Brendan McLoughlin  

Nathan Field has written an interesting and challenging book for anyone who practises psychotherapy. In many respects what he has to say is not essentially new though it is cogently expressed and arises from the twin sources of his own clinical experience and from the unfolding story of psychoanalysis throughout the century.

He starts his argument from the simple observation made early in his professional life, that there are at times developments in therapeutic work that cannot straightforwardly be explained in rational theoretical terms and which the therapist may not claim to have caused. In doing this he immediately removes the practitioner from a position of supposed objectivity and expertise and places him as an inclusive element in the therapeutic phenomenon. In doing so Field points beyond the medical-scientific frame of the origins of psychoanalysis to its roots in ancient healing and shamanistic traditions associated with religion. From this perspective, psychoanalysis may be seen not so much as a new therapeutic instrument but as a rediscovering and reframing of archaic human knowledge and understanding under the contemporary cloak of scientific rationalism.

Using a broad definition of the concept of breakdown he develops the familiar Jungian view of its teleological aspects and constructs on this his theory of fourth dimensionality.

John Southgate

John Southgate

Centre for Attachment-Based Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy

John Southgate  

My personal introduction to clinical questions about Multiple Personality was around 1987 when I took some drawings by a patient of mine to my supervisor, John Bowlby, at the Tavistock Clinic. This woman, he said, I think may be a multiple personality, to which I replied, ‘A what?’ He continued by saying that there was a lot of literature on this in the USA. It would have been good if I could have magically obtained Mollon's book at the time.

This is a timely book that will be of great value to clinicians whether or not they work with people who might be at the extreme end of the continuum of multiple personality dissociative identity disorder. Many patients suffer from milder forms of -dissociation and I would therefore recommend this book to all practising therapists. In addition this book is based on experience in the UK as Phil Mollon is based at the Lister Hospital, Stevenage, and trained as a clinical psychologist at Leeds and in psychoanalytic psychotherapy at the Tavistock Clinic. Many of the increasing number of books and articles are based on experience in the USA and, though Mollon faithfully examines this material, the clinical examples, which gratifyingly are numerous, are from a population we work with in this country.

The book starts with a discussion of dissociation, then reconsiders Freud's views of trauma, and looks at the work of the French pioneer and contemporary of Freud, Pierre Janet (Piaget's tutor). He then uses his background as a self psychologist to examine the effects of trauma and abuse on the developing self. In subsequent chapters he examines internal and external object relations and belief systems including how psychobiological processes react to the impact of trauma. He discusses contemporary work on memory and how this effects multiple personality, and works out how we can model what is happening in severe cases. There are practical explanations for clinicians on technique, the limitations of traditional approaches, dangers of retraumatization, relating to alters (separate internal selves), transference and countertransference, and adjunctive therapies. Then there is a composite fictitious case with a thorough discussion. He has some original thoughts about the nature of evil.

Dementia: An Intimate Death

Jane Garner

This paper focuses on the loss of intimacy and mutuality in the relationship when one partner has Alzheimer's disease and suggests that the paradigm of anticipatory grief described in terminal care work may need to be reconsidered in relation to organic brain disease. An attempt is made to link some of the psychoanalytic literature of grief and the experience of clinicians in old age psychiatry working with patients and their relatives. Mention is made of implications for management. The paper includes illustrative clinical material.



British Journal of Medical Psychology70, 149-157, 1997

Interpersonal Problems among Patients Suffering from Panic Disorder with Agoraphobia before and after Treatment

Asle Hoffart

The aim of this study was to examine interpersonal problems among panic disorder with agoraphobia patients before and after treatment. Patients (N = 46) suffering from panic disorder with moderate or severe agoraphobia and considering agoraphobia as their main problem were randomly assigned to receive either cognitive therapy or guided mastery therapy in a six-week in-patient group programme. The Inventory of Interpersonal Problems (IIP) and various symptom measures were administered at pre-treatment and at one-year follow-up. Two IIP subscales were derived from factor analysis of the present data: affiliation problems and power problems. The overall pattern of results supported a state model of interpersonal problems. At pre-treatment, the scores on the affiliation problems subscale were clearly related to nonspecific state characteristics, that is, to depression and general anxiety. From pre-treatment to follow-up, levels of interpersonal problems decreased significantly. Pre-treatment depression was a powerful predictor of change in interpersonal problems from pre-treatment to one-year follow-up. On the other hand, interpersonal problems at pre-treatment failed to predict the change in levels on various symptom scales.

On Sounds, Children, Identity and a ‘Quite Unmusical’ Man

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

38 Berkeley Road, London N8 8RU

Andrea Sabbadini  

In this article I explore, in the context of general psychoanalytic considerations about creativity, the specific place of music in human development. With reference to early auditory experiences, I emphasize the central place that sounds occupy in the formation of a child's separate identity. My thoughts on this subject also give me the opportunity for looking at some aspects of the complex relationship between music and psychoanalysis - two exquisitely auditory experiences - and for providing a historical review of Freud's own ambivalent attitude to music.

Publication of the Royal College of Psychiatrists' guidelines for provision of psychotherapy training for general psychiatric trainees led to the implementation of the pilot scheme described in this paper. Sherly Williams

Sherly Williams  

The paper proposes that the way therapists think about endings in psychotherapy is inseparable from the ends that they and their patients arrive at. At first, the question of how ends and endings relate would seem quite straightforward: determine the ‘criteria for termination’, and we will know how to effect the ending. In fact, it turns out to be quite the opposite: grapple with the ending as a central organizing phantasy underpinning the therapeutic relationship, and gradually the ends emerge. Particular attention is given to ‘ending’ as an archetype activated by the very nature of the therapeutic relationship.

This article is about the location of meaning and ‘truth’ in what our clients say. The concept of cover story is outlined and this is then applied to a ‘Freudian slip’. Various positions we take relative to the story are outlined. This is followed by three imaginary analyses by Freud, Laing and Lacan which demonstrate how the locus of truth can vary depending on our approach. The discussion of Lacan compares him favourably with many postmodernists, for whom the notion of truth has slipped away altogether.

Giambattista Vico (1668-1744) and Freud both claim to have discovered a ‘new science’ of the human. On Strategic Misreading of Ferenczi: A Reply to Piers Myers

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton

24-31 The Market, Greenwich, London SE10 9HZ

Martin Stanton  

Since his death in May 1933, Ferenczi's work has suffered from various misreadings, most of them connected to judgements of his clinical practice. Ernest Jones (who underwent his ‘training analysis’ with Ferenczi) sketched out the base-line here by asserting that Ferenczi's later work was marked by a ‘mental disturbance (which) had been making rapid progress (with) violent paranoiac and even homicidal outbursts’ (Jones 1957, p. 190). Ferenczi's ‘mutual analysis’ and his reported willingness to hold and comfort distressed patients (sarcastically dismissed by Freud as the ‘kissing technique’) are cited as clinical examples of this ‘mental disturbance’. Even 30 years later, Peter Gay (1988) uncritically reproduces main aspects of the Jones line, dismissing Ferenczi's Clinical Diary, for example, as ‘woolly-minded, unworldly metaphysics’ (p. 581), and supporting Freud's view of Ferenczi's ‘Confusion of Tongues’ paper as ‘harmless, stupid, also inadequate’ (p. 583).

In the last five years, the publication of Ferenczi's Clinical Diary and two volumes of his Correspondence with Freud, as well as extensive original research on Ferenczi's life and work, have prompted a major critical re-evaluation of his importance. The ‘Ferenczi Renaissance’, as Emanuel Berman (1996) recently called it, has reestablished Ferenczi as a complex and sophisticated innovator, whose work pioneered the study of transference and countertransference issues in traumatic process, and whose ‘technical experiments’ consciously highlighted the special needs of dissociatively disordered people in analysis.

Piers Myers (1996), in a recent article in this Journal, surprisingly ignores this ‘Renaissance’ and portrays a simplistic, if ‘tenacious’ Ferenczi, whose later clinical work fell into difficulty over ‘boundary’ issues. To add insult to injury, Myers even suggests that Robert Langs would have produced different results with Ferenczi's patients and, indeed, that the patients' reported dream and associative material itself indicates such a conclusion. Myers is either ignorant of the published biographical research on these patients, or chooses to ignore it. He uses Jeffrey Masson (1984) to substantiate that the patient RN in the Clinical Diary is Elizabeth Severn (Myers 1996, p. 29), but fails to note Masson's gross errors and misinformation about Severn. Masson suggested, for example, that Severn was a dancer whereas it was her daughter who was the dancer-and likewise the portrait he includes of Severn is also not of her but of her daughter. In fact, Severn was a practising psychotherapist (who worked for some time in London)

Response to Chris Purnell's Article: An Attachment-Based Approach to Working with Clients Affected by Hiv and Aids

Jill Brown

Jill Brown

The Harbour, 30 Frogmore Street, Bristol BSI 5NA

Jill Brown  

I have worked in HIV services during the past decade and for the past five years I have been running a small psychodynamic counselling service for people affected by HIV, AIDS and other life-threatening conditions. I was, therefore, very interested to read Chris Purnell's (1996) paper in which he describes his work with people affected by HIV and AIDS and looks at the relevance of attachment theory. I agree that Bowlby's ideas about attachment and the concept of a secure base are very helpful in understanding our clients' early attachment figures and how those experiences can be enacted with us. The provision of a secure base seems to me to be essential and fundamental in any kind of therapy which is successful in its reliability and its capacity to contain. The crisis of HIV or AIDS may intensify the need for the secure base for some clients which is perhaps what Purnell is stressing in his paper. I would like to respond to some of Purnell's ideas by indicating the difficulties and challenges in working with this group and finally by describing my work with a client at the end of his life.

Purnell describes a number of different approaches which he takes with clients, some of which I think arise from powerful countertransference feelings and perhaps from the primitive anxieties which are provoked in this work. With some clients Purnell feels he needs to offer a shoulder to cry on rather than offering counselling because these clients equate counselling and therapy with problems. Avoiding the problem focus of counselling or therapy in this way could be a collusion with the client's denial of the pain he or she is in. I am reminded of a paper by Coleman and Etchegoyen (1992) which examines the powerful effect on staff of patients in a STD clinic. They noticed that alongside ‘the patients' insatiable demand for exclusive care’ was the defensive denial of severe problems in relation to dependence and loss. There is throughout Purnell's paper an attempt to be all things for his clients so that sometimes he is masking his therapy, sometimes he is working exclusively within the external relationship system of the client, sometimes he is needing to validate his client's sadomasochistic relationship (because nobody else does), sometimes he is pursuing his angry and upset client who leaves the session early and, finally, he is attending to the emotional, physical and spiritual needs of his dying client. It sounds and feels like extremely hard work which is perhaps driven by anxiety and, possibly, by a need to counter the negative transference.

Who Speaks? Who Listens? Different Voices and Different Sexualities

Mary Ellis

Mary Ellis

78 Huddleston Road, London N7 0EG

Mary Ellis  

Psychoanalytic theories of sexuality have regarded homosexuality as a symptom of arrested sexual development. Such theorizing fails to acknowledge the prejudicial values that underpin it. The work of the philosopher, Michel Foucault, can offer psychotherapists new possibilities of considering sexual orientation that do not presuppose a split between the psychic and the socio-political. The complexity and diversity of lesbian roles, identities, experiences and cultures are particularly highlighted by Audre Lorde (a Black lesbian feminist theorist). The two cases illustrate how a Foucauldian analysis, combined with a psychoanalytic approach, can enable us to respond more sensitively to questions of identity in our work with patients.

The Generation of Psychoanalytic Knowledge: Sociological and Clinical Perspectives Part Two: Projective Identification-the other Side of the Equation

Sue Reid

Sue Reid

15 Pandora Road, London, NW6 1TS

Sue Reid  

Michael Rustin has proposed that the equivalent of Pasteur's ‘laboratory’ in psychoanalytic research has traditionally been the consulting room. It has been the consulting room that contributors to the development of psychoanalytic thinking have turned for evidence of psychoanalytic phenomena. It has become accepted as ‘good science’ within the field of psychoanalysis that new ideas should be supported by clinical evidence in the form of case material. There has also been a long psychoanalytic tradition of turning to literature for further support or elucidation of some aspect of unconscious life (the poets saw it first) and, of course, it may be that a poem, novel or play first sensitizes the clinician to clinical phenomena that he or she is currently struggling with, or, that it makes suddenly transparent something that seemed previously opaque.

But it has traditionally been the consulting room where hard evidence has been found or sought, where codification and purification of procedures have been developed. I would like to propose that material from psychoanalytic infant observation, as originated by Esther Bick (1964), be considered equivalent to case material from clinical work, both in its potential for the generation of new ideas, amending current theoretical constructs and clinical technique, but also with regard to the specification and standardization of what takes place in the infant observation setting.

The setting for psychoanalytic infant observation is prescribed just as it is in clinical work: one hour on a particular day of the week is negotiated with the observed family. The requirements of the observer are also clear: the observer should not give advice, influence the family's behaviour, initiate interactions or look after the baby. The observer, like the analyst, is not responsible for what unfolds (in infant observation, the unconscious interpersonal relationships between infant and other family members) but the observer is responsible, like the analyst in the consulting room, for struggling to take in what is seen and heard, and to allow it to have a life in the mind and then, subsequently, to record in as much detail as possible after the observational hour. To each setting psychoanalytically informed thinking is brought, characterized by a wish to understand unconscious phenomena and a recognition of the importance of valuing what is not understood.

In two Minds about Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy: Talking to Patients about Why They Do Not Do Their Homework

Paul March

Paul March

Harlesden Road, London NW10 3RY

Paul March  

In this paper I use three case studies to describe my attempts to understand and discuss with patients the difficulties that they often experience when trying to carry out tasks that have arisen from a collaborative relationship between us in cognitive-behavioural therapy. The difficulties seem to appear because of a conflict between two quite different views of the predicted outcome of collaboration. The conflict can occur both within patient and therapist as well as between them. I suggest that it can be understood by use of the concept of internal cohabitation (Sinason 1993; Richards 1993, 1994, 1995), the premise of which is that each human body contains two autonomous minds. One mind has the capacity to collaborate and develop, while the other believes only ill can come from such a venture.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Wilfred Bion has proved to be one of the most original psychoanalytic thinkers after Freud, furthering our understanding of psychotic processes and providing a framework for conceptualizing the development of thought, truth and mental growth. Bion's influence on psychoanalysis and psychotherapy has steadily grown; for example, who does not debate with himself how much ‘memory and desire’ to bring to bear in a session? Bion's notions of alpha function and beta elements and the metabolizing of toxic mental contents, under the rubric ‘nameless dread’, have enhanced the idea of working through, and his emphasis on the container/contained, attacks on linking and facing psychic pain has reshaped our thinking. Furthermore, all analytic schools have taken up Bion's elaborations on the importance of thinking and the various interferences with it. His scheme, outlined in the Grid, is an open system that allows us to envision how mental transformation is possible, and it is surprising that research models founded on his classification scheme to measure changes in thought patterns after psychoanalytic treatment have not been designed.

The 100th anniversary of Bion's birth in 1897 gives us an opportunity to celebrate his work with a Centenary Conference, held jointly with the Freud Museum in May 1997, and the publication of papers herein. Our distinguished speakers included Parthenope Bion Talamo who practises psychoanalysis in Italy. Her erudite analysis of her father's work and her spontaneous, witty remarks gave us clarity and insight into Bion's thinking and showed her to be her father's daughter. In the talk by Donald Meltzer, given without text and transcribed here, we were treated to a Bionic experience of the unfolding, gathering and deepening momentum of ideas, illustrating the place of ‘pre-conception’ and ‘the cloud of unknowing’ in giving birth to thought and object relations. This is the aesthetic experience which Meltzer considers to be the basis of creativity, the ‘toleration of the impact of the wondrous beauty of the parental couple’. Then, in David Taylor's paper there was an examination of the epistemological urge, the natural, inborn drive to learn and to know, and how this can be distorted or made ineffective. To counter the assault on ways of knowing, the Oedipus complex is essential. Dr Taylor's paper will be published next year in the Journal, a substitute appearing in this issue concerning how Bion arrives at meaning and understanding. In the final paper, David Bell spoke of the difference between neurotic and psychotic thinking. The toleration of frustration is the key, and the aim is to modify frustration, not to evade it or just bear it. This enables the distinction to be made between internal and external reality. With too much frustration, hatred of knowing or ‘minus K’ can appear to break links between self and object, between inner and outer. For reasons of clinical confidentiality Dr Bell's paper was unfortunately not available for publication.

In a survey of 422 psychoanalysts, 287 (68 per cent) reported data regarding 1222 homosexual patients. The database was analysed in regard to variables relating to the outcome of analysis. Change to heterosexuality was associated with the analyst's expectation that such change will occur. Significant therapeutic benefit was associated with greater length of analysis. Nearly two-thirds of patients received significant therapeutic benefit, without changing to heterosexuality. Higher rates of change were associated with higher rates of benefit for male patients. There is something rather disconcerting about the sequence in which the material is presented. After a brief description of the patient's subjective experience, a clear statement of the therapist's position is made: ‘I came to a diagnosis of paranoid-schizoid anxiety with manic defence’. This seems to tell us as much about the therapist as the client, situating her firmly in the Kleinian tradition, and one wonders if the diagnosis was made as early in the therapy as in the paper. There follows a certain amount of historical background which very sympathetically stresses the elements of early deprivation and specific trauma. This, and selected elements of her current reality (the difficulties with colleagues), are woven together with transference aspects to form a strand that traces the vicissitudes of the patient's aggression: her ‘feeling thoroughly persecuted by her bad objects’.

It is easy enough to speculate about alternative theoretical frameworks, especially when, unlike the therapist, one does not have the direct experience of the relationship with the client. But as the patient's history and preoccupations came to be elaborated, I found myself wondering if a formulation of the source of her paralysing anxiety might not be made in terms derived from Fairbaim's ideas about schizoid mechanisms. The therapeutic task would then revolve around exploring the patient's fear, not that her hate had killed her mother, but that her love was bad. For in spite of the Kleinian terminology, there is much in the material, including some of the therapist's interventions, to suggest that the patient fears her constructive and loving impulses have been and still are unavailing; and the assumption that the enemy here is the patient's projected hate, as opposed to an environment that cannot receive her love, is not necessarily borne out.

The elaborated version of the pin and bow incident, in which she finds her mother ‘sitting cross-legged in bed in a mad state’, speaks of a terror that the therapist finds almost unbearable. It seems that this terror derives from the sense that her mother cannot be reached, that her love is powerless or rejected. She says at this point: ‘I should never have been left alone with her’, as if she is beginning to see that this was too much to ask of a child's love (as the therapist confirms for her later: ‘it was not her job to make her mother better’) There is an even more harrowing instance of this failure to reach her mother in her earlier account of being sent up with a cup of tea, only to find her mother dead. But the story of the gift has been described as a ‘possible attempt at reparation’, suggesting that aggressive impulses lay beyond these actions. Similarly, what the patient talks about in relation to her colleague X is her fear of not being able to withstand X's hostility: ‘I deflate internally in the face of hostility’ - not her fear of doing damage by her own anger, which is what is offered in interpretation. She is afraid that, if X's ‘vision of the world operated everywhere, this institution would have been on the rocks years ago’.

Richard Tan

Richard Tan

Member, Centre for Psychoanalytical Psychotherapy (CPP)

Richard Tan  

The interface between giving clinical comments and supervising a case is a very fine one. Thus it is inevitable that the commentator appears at times to be supervising the presenter. I therefore approach this task with some ambivalence.

In writing this commentary, I will firstly comment about this case in the general and, secondly, some ideas specific to the material presented in the sessions. A clinical commentary is always difficult to write with clarity because it is one stage removed from the heat of the moment when psychotherapist and patient are engaged in a dynamic relationship. On the other hand, although we are deprived of the immediacy of feelings and responses, we do have the luxury of time and space to reflect and think about the implications of the exchanges in the sessions reported.

In our work as psychoanalytic psychotherapists since the 1950s onwards, we have come to rely on our countertransference feelings in the broad sense to inform our thinking about the patient's internal object relations. How we are present or not present in the mind of the patient, and the reverse situation of how he is kept in ours, the way the patient is using us alongside and beyond what he is saying - these are important indications of the patient's functioning.

Paul Williams

Paul Williams

British Psycho-Analytical Society, London

Paul Williams  

There has been a growth in interest over the past 20 years in Buddhist psychology and its links with psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Many books have appeared and a reader fresh to the subject might be forgiven for feeling confused at their range and varied quality. An exception is Walpola Rahula's What the Buddha Taught. Although not concerned with psychotherapy directly, this classic introduction to the Buddhist mind will resonate with any interested psychotherapist. Mark Epstein, a psychiatrist, psychotherapist and Buddhist, has achieved something similar in that he conveys the emotional foundations of Buddhist practice, but in addition he has managed to link these to psychoanalytic theory and clinical work without reductionism or damage to either. This is no small achievement. An ordinariness and clarity of approach combined with. scholarly thinking characterize the work. This is exemplified by a simple story of a dharma combat (the clashing of great minds sharpened by years of study and meditation) arranged by Epstein between two monks, Kalu Rinpoche of Tibet and the Korean Zen Master Seung Sahn. The latter, renowned for insistence on the importance of a ‘don't know mind’, reached into his robes and drew out an orange. ‘What is this?’ he demanded of the lama, ready to pounce on any answer. Kalu Rinpoche bent to the Tibetan monk next to him who was acting as translator, and they whispered together. Eventually the translator addressed the packed room: ‘Rinpoche says, “What is the matter with him? Don't they have oranges where he comes from?”’ The dialogue ended.

As the emphasis on sexual and aggressive strivings in therapy has given way to a focus on how individuals are unhappy in fundamental ways with who they are, so the subject of the self has emerged as the focus of Buddhism and psychoanalysis. In ten chapters divided into three parts (Buddhist Psychology, Meditation, Therapy) Epstein explores how both disciplines - Buddhism and psychoanalytic therapy - approach neurotic strivings by addressing the problematic of the self and procedures for the freeing of ego functions attached to it. In the first part he depicts the Buddha's psychological teachings in the language of Western psychodynamics. In the second, he links Buddhist meditation to psychoanalysis via the strategy of ‘bare attention’, a concept Freud and Bion would have recognized immediately.

Ken Wright  

This very unusual book is the story of one man's search for salvation. This in itself is not an unusual theme but, because the person concerned was an influential and innovative psychoanalyst, the story immediately acquires a new dimension. It provides a unique opportunity - unique at least in the sense of being public - to see how important advances in theoretical understanding are linked to fundamental life problems of the analyst.

In one sense we know this already. From Freud's self-analysis, for example, we know that his discovery of, and monolithic emphasis on, the Oedipus complex was linked to his own unresolved pathology in this area. I think we are also beginning to know that many of the early schisms in psychoanalysis, and perhaps the later ones as well, were at least partly based on the differing pathologies - and hence differing sensitivities - of the dissident analysts.

Notwithstanding, this is not the official view. This still regards the analyst as one who quasi-objectively surveys his patients' pathologies, in turn making sense of them in terms of established theories.
