Ian Simpson

Ian Simpson

London

Ian Simpson  

This book presents an overview of some of the current work being done with men in the USA. Its main focus is on groupwork but much of what is on offer is relevant to the wider issue of men and mental health. Traditionally, and this is the starting point for most of the contributors, men have not taken to psychotherapy as have women. Psychotherapy may have originally been undertaken by male professionals primarily for women patients but, in general, men themselves have been more reluctant to see themselves as patients. The stereotypical male is independent, self-reliant, strong and emotionally restrained. Historically, this has meant that many have been resistant to therapy and what it could offer. However this has been changing over the past few decades. For instance, since the advent of the women's movement, gender stereotypes have been challenged and men have been forced to face the consequences. Some men have found that they need to seek alternative ways to combat the feelings of alienation and anxiety that have confronted them as their familiar roles have changed. In recent years the mythopoetic men's movement, most clearly represented by the work of Robert Bly, bears witness to this striving for a better understanding of what it means to be a man today. This book attempts to follow on from these popular developments by outlining the work of some mental health professionals who are currently involved with men and men's issues.

Men In Groups is organized into four parts. Each part typically contains chapters on psychotherapy and supportive and educational groupwork. Throughout, particular attention is paid to cultural and social factors and the way in which these influence and affect working with men. The first section looks at homogeneous all-male groups, including treatment for therapy-resistant men, homeless men, middle-class men and Asian men, and at mentoring groups. Section two concentrates on heterogeneous and mixed-gender groups. This includes work with African American, Hispanic and gay men, but also looks at men's work from a female therapist's perspective and at the exploration of sexism in mixed groups. The third section is devoted to issues of fathering and being fathered, while section four looks at the ‘darker’ side of men and explores groupwork with alcohol-dependent men, men who are violent or sexually abusive, and men who have been traumatized. The latter group includes men suffering from PTSD and men who have been sexually abused.

Brett Kahr's book D. W. Winnicott: A Biographical Portrait is, by the author's own admission, a sketch. It is an annotated book of facts and details concerning the life of Donald Winnicott. As such, it leaves the reader hanging-we want to know more. For those students perhaps only just beginning to encounter the work of Winnicott, the book does serve to give quite extensive factual background information as to what Winnicott achieved, when and how he achieved it, as well as a clear picture of the psychoanalytic climate at the time. But it begs many questions. Brett Kahr is currently working on a fuller biography which may or may not go some way towards answering some of the many questions that the book provokes.

It has to be asked why the author decided to publish this book when by the very nature of it being a sketch it is unsatisfactory. Sketches are all very well but rarely do they satisfy us, we want a fuller picture. There is of course the odd rare exception where a biographical sketch goes far enough to convey something of the essence of the man: Norman Malcolm's book on Wittgenstein, for example. It is, however, clear from this book that Brett Kahr has enormous respect and admiration for this complex, modest man. It is lovingly written though he can sometimes be rather formal in his use of language. He keeps himself rigidly to the facts and very rarely dares to conjecture.

Biographies are strange affairs. We read them not only because we like reading stories but because we are curious. A biography should seek to give us a fuller, more tangible picture of a person by linking the outer events of life with the more complex, inner world. Writing a biography sets the author on a trail of detective work, finding out the facts, then linking them together with intuition and imagination-putting flesh on the bones so to speak.

For those of us engaged in a serious and sustained study of the work of D.W. Winnicott this book has little to offer. Much of the information it contains can easily be gleaned from other sources (Clare Winnicott, Masud Khan, Marion Milner, Alexander Newman). The author states in his preface (p. xxix), ‘This book is not an attempt to review Winnicott's work nor a critical account of his ideas and their influences.’ But surely somewhere Winnicott's use of irony deserves a mention, not least because his way of using irony is integral to his character. To describe Winnicott as having ‘unparalleled succinctness’ when he (Winnicott) describes Strachey as ‘not a great man-he will always be my favourite example of a psychoanalyst’ is surely to miss the point. Juliet Miller  

I approached this book anticipating a sympathetic and straightforward guide to the basics of practising as a psychotherapist. Both the title and the cover of the book encouraged me in this idea. Instead I found I was grappling with a very different and sometimes strange book. A Safe Place is a mixture of anecdotal musings and clinical material interwoven in a rather uncomfortable way with an attempt to explain and justify the profession of psychotherapy. The author is Professor of Psychiatry at Harvard Medical School, and I finally decided that this book is written for students of psychiatry who are sceptical about the field of psychotherapy. The book is written as if the field of psychotherapy was a foreign and unknown territory to the reader.

The author says, however, that he writes for the general reader as much as for the professional, but on two readings of this book I found it difficult to relate to from the point of view either of a psychotherapist or a general reader. It is a book which is wide ranging in its attempt to draw on the psychoanalytic psychotherapies, psychiatry and the social sciences, but as it is a short book the author is unable to develop these ideas fully. The author places some clinical material in each of his chapters and then weaves a discourse around each one, encompassing bits of theory, speculations on the reader's understanding of psychotherapy and brief historical reviews of the history of psychoanalysis, all of which adds up to an uncomfortable patchwork with no overall design.

There are four sections to the book whose titles suggest common overall themes to the chapters: ‘Making a safe place’, ‘Reinventing the interview’, ‘Dangerous places’ and ‘Today and tomorrow’. This categorizing feels like an attempt to draw together some very scattered ideas. In ‘Making a safe place’ we have one chapter describing the author's work with a patient for whom a safe place is a place without interpretations. There is also a brief look at Freud and what the author calls his passive stance, and a chapter in which he discusses the therapeutic use of performative statements.

In 1900 a young woman called Ida Bauer -‘Dora’-was brought by her father to see Sigmund Freud. Her father was Freud's patient; he had treated him for syphilis with which he had infected his wife. The husband of his mistress had recently claimed that Dora had falsely accused him of making sexual advances to her. For this and other reasons, her hysterical symptoms had intensified. Freud took her into treatment. It was not a success.

Freud strove to persuade Dora that if she could acknowledge her sexual attraction to her father, his mistress and her husband, her hysterical symptoms would disappear, as, indeed, some of them did.

36 Essex Park, London N3 1 NE

Patsy Ryz  

Writing a commentary on ‘blind’ material is a tantalizing experience because it presents one with a host of questions that cannot be answered. This could well be inherent in the Clinical Commentary medium but it could also be a reflection of this particular piece of material which describes a very early stage of an intervention when things are bound to be quite unknown to the therapist.

Be that as it may, I cannot help wondering how the background information was selected. Was it left entirely at the therapist's discretion or were there criteria to be followed? For example, were facts selected on ‘a need to know’ basis? This in turn raises further questions. How much does one need to know in order to make informed comments? And how far can one separate clinical material per se from the external framework within which it occurs?

Lydia's referral has a disjointed quality to it. As we learn more about Lydia and her baby it becomes clear that this disconnection mirrors something of the relationship between them. We hear that Lydia's 7-year-old son, Jay, is in once-weekly therapy for depression (mother's symptom but an unusual one for a 7-year-old); and yet Lydia is, apparently, referred incidentally, due to the alarm she causes in the waiting-room rather than within the context of Jay's therapy when parental support might have been considered and set up. This seems odd given Lydia's history which presumably was known at the time of Jay's referral. Was help initially offered but refused by her? Perhaps the psychiatric input she was already receiving was felt to be sufficient for her needs? Or was the Unit's response mirroring an aspect of the family dynamics whereby Lydia gets bypassed and overlooked, with the Unit taking over Jay in the same way that maternal grandmother (MGM) takes over mother's role?

We hear something about the psychiatrist but not much about the nature of the intervention. What form did the weekly visits take? Who was present? How do we understand Lydia's reported lack of interest in her four children? The psychiatrist, unlike the counsellor, was apparently unable to kindle Lydia's interest in her offspring. Was this because the visits took place at home - perhaps in MGM's presence? Has Lydia ever felt ‘at home’ as a mother in her own right and, particularly, in her own mother's eyes? Lydia does not take the medication prescribed for her depression.

Meg Sharpe

Meg Sharpe

London

Meg Sharpe  

What is a dream? What part does it play in everyday life? Although many people are curious about their dreams, the subject tends to be given low priority in our society apart from professionals who struggle to understand their psychic meaning. However, symbolic awareness has increased in the last decades and, with an increase in dream seminars and lectures and more people entering therapy, there is a greater interest in unconscious material.

Dr Montague Ullman is a distinguished New York psychoanalyst and Clinical Professor Emeritus in Psychiatry at Albert Einstein College of Medicine. Like S.H. Foulkes, the founder of British group analysis, his varied background includes service in the army during World War II. Research interests led him to explore the neurophysiological, clinical and social aspects of dreaming. He is the author and coauthor of many books on this topic and this current one is to help confirm ‘oneirophiles’ (lovers of dreams!) as well as encouraging new recruits. This book, a product of over 20 years' research and practice, is a reference manual with specialized chapters to assist those who are already interested and involved in leading dream groups. He spent many years working out a technique which is informative, original and interesting. He is well known in the US and Scandinavia where he has conducted master classes in this field. Certainly one or other of his disciples will always be found at the annual convention of the American Group Psychotherapists.

Ullman originally devised his technique as a strategy in training psychoanalysts. However, it has proved to be of interest to many non-professionals. His method is designed for groups and is at the same time intensely personal to the individual dreamer, but, in the hands of a skilled practitioner, does not encroach on the individual's integrity. Thus, whilst it emphasizes a group approach, it can equally be utilized by an individual choosing to work on his/her own. The book takes us in depth into the skills he has developed, and its 18 chapters are easily readable and contain a wealth of clinical illustrations.

Cheryl Moskowitz  

Reading Marina Jenkyns' The Play's the Thing is like being taken out to the theatre and treated to wine, dinner and conversation afterwards with lively and intelligent company. Her book manages to be scholarly without being purely academic and

120

specialized without being elitist. It is the sort of encounter which leaves you feeling full and satisfied with the promise that many of its moments may be savoured for some time to come.

Marina Jenkyns is a therapist who is driven to use drama in her work not, it would seem, because some aspect of her training may have prescribed its application as required technique but rather because, at some very deep level, she is in love with the play itself as well as being passionate about it as an inexhaustible tool for selfunderstanding. She tells us in her prologue:

The characters and life of any text open to us the moment we open the book. They sleep till we come. They can waken to us over and over and over again. Each time we encounter a text we bring to it… not only our conscious but also our unconscious life. So we do in dramatherapy. As the child in the drama class does. As the actor does. As the audience does. (p. xi)

Her passion for the text, the play, is infectious. To ensure the less Thespian reader is not left floundering Jenkyns supplies a detailed synopsis of plot and breakdown of characters for each work she explores. Thus armed it is practically impossible not to follow with the same breathless excitement as she journeys through play after play combining a detailed personal analysis with colourful accounts of practical application with participants in dramatherapy group settings. She permits the reader audience with her own internal monologue as well as those of the characters in the plays and the participants in the groups. The way that Marina Jenkyns works with text is much as an analyst does with a patient, staying with the material, allowing the story to unfold and applying gently but firmly the probing of a tooth-comb to uncover the most useful and productive truths.

Joanna Ryan  

This book is an extremely valuable and refreshing contribution to the debate about psychoanalysis and homosexuality. Although almost entirely American, it speaks most appositely to the charged and complex nature of similar discussions in the UK. It contains a challenging mixture of accounts from lesbian and gay analysts and therapists of their experiences at the cutting edge of psychoanalytic homophobia, combined with discussions of what theoretical and clinical innovations are needed to provide more adequate psychoanalytic approaches to homosexuality. The three chapters of personal accounts (Drescher, Goldman/Schaffner, and Martin), of lesbian and gay analysts experiencing and struggling with professional exclusion, discrimination and prejudice, are in themselves essential documents in this shaming aspect of the history of psychoanalysis. But these records also allow us to appreciate the courage and integrity of the authors in the other sections of this book who have overcome the many hurtful and crushing aspects of psychoanalytic homophobia to do innovative, creative, and respectful analytic work with their lesbian and gay patients, and also put forward new theoretical critiques and ideas.

This difficult insistence on the value of psychoanalysis in the face of its pathologizing of homosexuality is at its most acute in Domenici's thoughtful and detailed chapter on Fairbairn's theories, which should be of great interest to many object-relations therapists in this country. Fairbairn is notorious (although perhaps this is not so widely known) for suggesting that homosexuals should be segregated into settlement camps. He regarded homosexuals as psychopaths, incapable of healthy relationships. Domenici traces the origin of this in Fairbairn's particular use of the notions of exciting and rejecting objects in oedipal structures. He argues that Fairbairn is not true to his own relational position at certain crucial points, and tries to develop some of Fairbairn's ideas further to account for anti-homosexuality, and the heterosexuality that is based on this. He, like other authors in this book, uses the work of the feminist philosopher, Judith Butler, especially her far-reaching critiques of received conceptualizations of gender and desire.

Tim Fox

Tim Fox

London

Tim Fox  

Harold Stewart's book, published in The New Library of Psychoanalysis Series (Volume 25), provides a stimulating and admirably clear account of Michael Balint's contribution to psychoanalysis and applied psychoanalysis as well as painting an absorbing picture of Balint himself.

After a brief biographical sketch and a useful introductory summary, the author describes and examines the development of Balint's theoretical concepts drawn from his clinical experience with patients, and shows how, concurrently with these ideas and experiences, Balint refined his views on analytic technique. He shows how central to these developments was Balint's contention that from the earliest beginnings the infant exists and develops in a state of intense relatedness to his environment. Building on the work of Ferenczi, Balint was among the first to envisage regression as a therapeutic tool, not solely as a defence, and how in favourable circumstances it may provide an opportunity for the individual to discover new ways of loving - Balint's

new beginning' - where healthy developments in relation to objects have miscarried.

Balint gradually moved away from his original concept of an early passive relationship to the primary object, postulating instead an earliest, primitive relationship of ‘harmonious mix-up’ of subject and object containing many active features. Out of this primitive relationship, which Balint termed ‘primary object love’, both normal and pathological paths of development arise as with birth, separation and inevitable frustrations the harmonious mix-up gives way to discrete objects. The author lucidly outlines the development of these ideas and the clinical importance Balint attached to them, from his earliest analytic writings to their fullest synthesis, as set out in The Basic Fault (1968). Here, Balint introduced his concept of a structural deficiency in the mind (the ‘basic fault’), arising from early and significant discrepancies between the bio-psychological needs of the infant and the provision of material and psychological care. He describes how Balint came to conceptualize the mind in terms of three areas - those of one-person (the area of creativity), two-person (the area of the basic fault) and three-person (the area of the Oedipus conflict) relationships - and outlines Balint's theories on trauma and on hate, which he saw not as a primary drive but always as a secondary and reactive phenomenon.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The burgeoning growth of attachment studies, based on Bowlby's model and developed by researchers such as Ainsworth, Main and Fonagy, has moved psychoanalytic research into alignment with experimental psychology, laying new groundwork for scientific respectability. This most welcome and much needed development in the research field enables predictions to be made about the attachment patterns of infants according to the parent's attachment history, illustrating how disturbed (or secure) relating is transmitted to the next generation. Attachment literature makes significant links with the clinical orientation when detailed observations of attachment behaviour are made in situ that can be applied to clinical understanding, as our first paper by Patricia Hughes and Gill McGauley shows. A mother and her infant were subjects in a large study of families in which a previous child had been stillborn, using videos of mother/infant interaction, the Strange Situation and the Adult Attachment Interview. Separately, weekly baby observations were made over the course of the first year with this vulnerable mother who had not resolved her own separation difficulties, nor sufficiently mourned her stillborn baby. The child was rated ‘avoidant’ and ‘disorganized’ in respect of attachment, observed vividly in interaction with a mother who was hostile and overstimulating towards her child, clearly signalling the type of pattern resulting from maternal unresolved loss that so often shows up in adults in psychotherapy. The potential for this research methodology to develop further in sophistication in observing and documenting not only attachment behaviours but other various types of object relations is immense, and hopefully will continue to grow, informing clinical work as well as further theory and research.

In our work with psychotherapy patients I suspect all practitioners apply their knowledge flexibly, according to the specific needs of the particular patient. As Bion said, one chooses the golf club in order to play the ball as it lies. However, psychotherapy debate is often carried on as if rigorous rules are applied across the board with all patients, as if therapists from different orientations rigidly adhere to a narrow range of theories in their work. Could it be that the formation of theoretical groups is more a reflection of the need for membership and tribal identity than an indication of intractable differences and production line treatments? One debate, regularly linked with various theoretical groups, comes to the fore again and again, and seems a false -dichotomy, attributing the psychogenic roots of pathology to either ‘the internal world’ or ‘the environment’, when interaction between the two seems such an obvious determinant. This complexity, of course, puts a greater demand on the thinking capacities of the psychotherapist. The tendency to polarize and to think in either/or terms is rife among psychotherapists (of all people!)

Response to Jeremy Holmes's Too Early, Too Late' - Countertransference and Endings

Dorothy Hamilton

Dorothy Hamilton

AGIP, 1 Fairbridge Rd., London N19 3EW

Dorothy Hamilton  

If we say someone has left too early or too late, we are clearly referring to the experience of the patient: we are making a therapeutic judgement about that person's inner state. But if we talk of a countertransference to the leaving, we are referring to the experience of the therapist who feels it is too early or too late, either because he or she is accurately attuned, or because - and this is the sense in which the term ‘countertransference’ is more likely to be used - he or she is caught perversely into some projection from the patient. I'm assuming here that most of us have arrived at some form of Hermann's definition of countertransference - that is, all our responses to a particular patient, responses which may be used both as a tool to understand the patient and as a monitor of the therapist's competence. In the matter of an ending that seems too early or too late, how can we distinguish between our countertransference and our therapeutic judgement?

Jeremy gives an attachment theory model for countertransference. Describing the establishment of a ‘secure base’, both in reality and as an internal representation within the patient, as the aim of attachment therapy, he says: ‘A secure base arises partly out of the responsiveness and attunement provided by the therapist, partly from her capacity to accept and metabolize protest and anger’. Responsiveness and attunement; the capacity to accept and metabolize protest and anger: that, I think, is a lovely description, both comprehensive and concise, of what many of us would call the ‘maternal reverie’ of the therapist.

The attachment theorist's ‘attunement’ may be likened to Freud's use of the unconscious receptive instrument; to the post-Kleinian ‘normal’ or healthy countertransference (perhaps based on ‘normal’ projective identifications from the patient); and, as Jeremy says, to Racker's ‘concordant’ countertransference. The words ‘accept and metabolize’ refer to the capacity to take the undigested material the patient fires at the therapist - Bion's beta elements - and convert it, through the therapist's alpha function, into digestible material. Too often, of course, our identifications become, in Racker's terms, complementary - we identify, not appropriately with the patient's feelings and needs, but with his or her internal objects. Then, in Bion's language again, we find ourselves firing back beta elements at the bewildered patient.

Martin Golding  

In the final section of this essay about her life as a child of survivors of the Holocaust, Anne Karpf exclaims: ‘I always felt that my life had been inflected around an event I'd never experienced’. Later, on a visit to Auschwitz, she recognizes an illusion: ‘as if coming in person to the site of terrible events which occurred fifty years ago could somehow yield them up for us to transform them - they might actually extrude through the stones and earth and be mitigated by modern sorrow’. The presence of the past has pervaded her life. Recognizing its separation from the present represents a culminating insight for the author, allowing her to accept that she can live with her ‘flawed and contingent accommodations’. The path to that insight is difficult for both the writer and the reader. The book's uncertainties, dissimulated in fluent and confident writing, created in this reviewer a sense of confusion which seemed to reflect the confusion of the original experience.

Anne Karpf's parents were Polish Jews. Her father was imprisoned by the Russians during the Nazi-Soviet partition, suffered great hardship, was released following Barbarossa, and spent the rest of the war behind Russian lines, anxious but relatively safe. Her mother, a virtuoso pianist, after terrible experiences in the ghetto of Tarnow was captured and, with her sister, survived successively Plash, Auschwitz, and Lichtewerden. Anne Karpf's parents met and married in Poland after the war, and eventually sought asylum in Britain, where both Anne and her elder sister were born. She records profound inner perplexity and self-division; of feeling engulfed by her parents' story and its implicit prescriptions; ‘umbilically’ attached to them, and responsible for their welfare; unable to enjoy emotional freedom, particularly to be angry with her parents, to be less than perfect for them. She began an affair with a non-Jewish man (which became eventually a settled relationship which has produced two daughters); but this provoked retaliation in the form of severe and chronic eczema, and led her to enter psychotherapy. Her identification with her parents' experience had been so overwhelming that their wartime perils seemed enacted in the ordinary fluctuations and risks of daily life: after visiting Auschwitz, Anne Karpf comments, ‘I think I had some ridiculous fantasy that at Auschwitz I might die’.

Bernard Barnett  

Ilany Kogan is a psychoanalyst working in Israel and researching into the problems of Holocaust survivors and their children, the so-called ‘Second Generation’. Over the last decade she has developed a specialized knowledge in this area and the fruits of her research, her published papers, have now been brought together and made more easily accessible in the The Cry of Mute Children. This book consists of seven chapters with a preface by Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel and an introduction and epilogue. Each chapter is centred on a detailed case study and includes a useful and well-informed discussion of the main theoretical and clinical issues.

The crux of Kogan's work is that the survivors and their families cannot mourn the Holocaust. Her (and other) research (Kestenberg 1993) suggests that some 50 years after World War II, the Holocaust cannot yet be mourned. The cold-blooded, calculated, efficient and brutal murder of millions of Jews, gypsies and other persons including a million and a quarter children has been historically noted. However, the enormity of the perpetrators' crime against humanity, the nature of the massive psychic trauma and the quality of the incalculable loss, cannot really be grasped. Indeed in our minds we cannot get much beyond the repetition of mere statistics or the recall of stark images, like piles of shoes and suitcases, that trouble and challenge the imagination and raise disturbing questions about the human condition. In the continuous search for the meaning of these terrible events we are also challenged by the accumulating body of evidence on the aftermath of the Holocaust, the after-effects which include the continued suffering of the survivors and the transmission of the parental trauma to their children and to their children's children.

It is this legacy of the Holocaust and its sequelae, the transmission of the trauma, that is Ilany Kogan's concern in The Cry of Mute Children.

This book is one of a series being published by the Analytic Press to try to promote serious consideration of the ideas of relational psychoanalysis which have been developing in recent years, particularly in New York. Lewis Aron is part of a group of analysts involved with the New York City Post-Doctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis: some of the better known thinkers around this grouping would include Jessica Benjamin, Michael Eigen and Stephen Mitchell. Aron is one of several linked to this group who have been trying to develop a theoretical underpinning for what he describes as a radical ‘relational’ psychoanalysis; and this book is really an attempt to give the reader a clear view of exactly what is unique about this perspective and, in the process, to think about how these ideas relate to and differ from more mainstream psychoanalytic views.

The first part of the book tells a story, an historical one, of the development of a way of thinking that has grown out of dissatisfaction with traditional ego-psychological theories and which attempts the challenge of integrating aspects of theories, as diverse as Kohut, British post-Kleinian and object relation perspectives, as well as the interpersonal tradition of Harry Stack Sullivan and the ‘intersubjective’ approach of Stolorow and his colleagues. He tries to link all this with ‘post-modern’ ideas in general, adding a dash of other luminaries such as Harold Searles and Schafer to create a heady brew indeed. Although at times bordering on the esoteric as he attempts to explore fine differentiations between theories which are little debated here, he does manage to guide the reader through the theoretical maze and lead us to the exposition of his particular position.

Some of the debate will not seem new to British readers, maybe in particular the need to embrace a two-person psychology. However he does argue firmly against what he sees as the positivist residues in psychoanalytic theory, in particular, the idea of the analyst as the healthy observer of the ill patient. The metaphor of the analytic space as a ‘pure culture’ in which the transference can develop is an anathema to Aron. He wants the psychotherapeutic endeavour to be conceived as a genuine interaction of two minds, two emotional worlds, and he argues strongly against the idea that a therapist can eliminate the effects of his own subjectivity and so be ‘neutral’. He is not just reiterating the now well accepted ideas about the need to take seriously the countertransference, but is arguing for the need to take equally seriously the impact of the personality and theories of the therapist on the minutiae of the therapeutic process. Following much contemporary scientific thought he stresses how the observer or therapist constructs, organizes and shapes what is observed.

Paul Williams  

The Book Reviews Editor of the BJP did not know, when she rang me to ask me to review this book, that Nina Coltart was my training analyst. I accepted the invitation without hesitation, but soon found myself experiencing the curious mixture of feelings one has when asked to comment on one's analyst's work: namely, the sense of feeling at the same time singularly qualified and unqualified to comment, both by virtue of the perspective granted by the role of analysand. This quandary remained, and shifted only when a forgotten comment by another analyst on Nina Coltart's work surfaced in my mind. This comment was: ‘Nina Coltart's students are all quite different. The fact that they've retained their individuality strikes me as being important.’ I realized that I could review this book from the standpoint of the Nina Coltart I know, which will not be the same as others' versions of her. I was then faced with a further problem: the Nina Coltart described in Kit Bollas's introduction to the book is not the Nina Coltart I knew. Kit's description is of a somewhat ethereal, slightly blue-stocking figure exuding spirituality. My experience of her was of a lively woman who possessed a remarkable ordinariness and unusual sanity. Perhaps something upon which many would agree is Coltart's clinical standing: she was, as Bollas points out, one of the great training analysts, supervisors, teachers and administrators at the Institute of Psycho-Analysis from the early 1970s through the mid-1990s when she retired from analytic life. This book, her last, demonstrates her clinical skill with the familiar clarity and textural complexity that characterizes her earlier publications. Yet this collection of papers is a signing-off. Reading them, one is left with the impression of an author saying goodbye by way of a series of late-in-life reflections upon past experiences and present values. I shall return to this; first, the papers.

Coltart opens with her membership paper for the British Psycho-Analytical Society. There is a slight formality about the paper but it demonstrates vividly her interest in clinical work which was to preoccupy her over the ensuing 30 years. The account of her perverse patient who was her membership case is characterized by intense involvement with his appalling difficulties, and is achieved with a lightness of touch that was one of her trademarks. This is a facet of Nina Coltart's work which confused me for a long time in my own analysis. I was very inexperienced, ignorant of what to expect in the analysis and naturally keen to learn as I had been accepted as a candidate for the psychoanalytic training. I could not fathom why she did not make profound or earth-shattering interpretations of my difficulties. At the same time, she would make comments which seemed almost conversational, so apparently simple were they; yet they seemed to dwell in my mind as puzzles.

Mario Jacoby came up with the idea of writing this book while reading Simenon. ‘Everyone has a shadow side’, Simenon had written, ‘of which he is more or less ashamed.’ Simenon, with his own secret past to hide, welcomed meeting people on the same plane as himself, with similar symptoms and similar shame, as it made him feel less alone, ‘less of a monster’.

Shame is, as Simenon points out, very much experienced on one's own - it generates a terrible loneliness. The ‘monster’ he cites takes us back to childhood where shame looms so large. Shame can then be overwhelming, a full-body invasion, accompanied by blushing and feelings of helplessness. No visible avenues of escape suggest themselves.

Jacoby's own personal experiences, both personally and professionally, are brought into play here and this personal angle lends weight and force to the book. In his preface he notes the difficulty of trying to pin down such a complex issue. He states, ‘the science of the psyche can never sufficiently encompass the kaleidoscopic richness and complexity of the living soul’ (p. ix). Soul gives an indication of the Jungian orientation of the book, though Jacoby fully covers other writers on the subject.

Jacoby's book is well timed since the significance of shame, often frequently underestimated, is on the increase. It's always said that we live in a guilt culture, characteristic of Western societies. Nowadays, as social structures collapse, the fear of being caught out on one's own, of shame, seems to be increasing. Indeed Jacoby alerts us to the prevalence of ‘shame-anxiety’, the anticipatory fear of being caught out, either through a mistake of one's own, or an omission, or even through too much enthusiasm. This can happen at all stages of therapy, but Jacoby notes how a new patient at the initial interview is often assailed with shame in revealing all to a stranger. He himself usually acknowledges this by verbalizing it, to the evident relief of the newcomer - a useful tip.

Shame brings with it humiliation and feelings of inferiority, and Jacoby gives many examples to illustrate this - a haunting one of a Swiss schoolboy on a school trip with a bag of cherries given to him by his doting mother, who suddenly finds himself caught short on the train and is forced to defecate in his pants, to the lasting derision of his fellow pupils. This experience marked him for life, both the suddenness of shame and the consequent and abiding loss of self-respect.

Introductory Notes on Wilfred Bion

Robin Anderson

Robin Anderson

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Robin Anderson  

Wilfred Bion was born in 1897 in Muttra, India, where his father was an engineer and administrator. India made a lasting impression on him and amongst the writings that he used in his work was the Bhagavad Gita. He was parted from his family at the young age of 8 to attend school in England as was the sad custom at that time. During the First World War he joined the Royal Tank Corps and saw a great deal of action for which he received two high awards for gallantry. In his later book The Long Week End (1982), though, Bion makes it clear that in the chaos and fear of war, what happens is very confused and unclear and is rewritten and falsified afterwards in an attempt to make sense of the madness. These experiences clearly influenced him deeply and one constantly sees them reflected in his psychoanalytical writings, especially on psychotic states. The extreme violence and fragmentation of psychotic projectiles and psychic landscapes in devastation and ruin seem to me to come straight from images of that terrible war. He went to Oxford where he excelled in sport and graduated in Modern History. After a brief period of teaching, and already interested in psychoanalysis, he went to University College Hospital to study medicine in order to pursue a career in psychoanalysis. One of his appointments was with Wilfred Trotter, a surgeon with a deep interest in psychology who was known for his book on groups, The Instincts of the Herd in Peace and War (1916), upon which Bion clearly drew in his work on groups. After qualifying he went straight into psychiatry and was soon working at the Tavistock Clinic and started analysis with John Rickman. His psychoanalytic training was interrupted by the Second World War, during which time he was very active in using and developing his ideas on groups in the treatment of psychological casualties as well as in the selection of officers and this early work with groups formed the subject of his first paper (Bion 1943). After the war he completed his psychoanalytic training in analysis with Melanie Klein, which had a profound influence on his development as an analyst. His radical work on groups arising out of his war work, and at the Tavistock Clinic (Bion 1961) gave way to more purely psychoanalytic study from the 1950s onwards. Along with a number of other Kleinian analysts at that time, notably Herbert Rosenfeld and Hanna Segal, he analysed many psychotic and borderline patients drawing especially on Melanie Klein's (1946) paper ‘Notes on some schizoid mechanisms’. This work formed the basis for several important papers, especially ‘The differentiation of the psychotic from the nonpsychotic personalities’ (Bion 1957), ‘On arrogance’ (Bion 1958) and ‘Attacks on linking’ (Bion 1959).

This sensitive and very readable book on the psychological experience of the child with a life-threatening illness is written by a Canadian psychologist. She describes her work as ‘psychotherapy’. She clearly is very experienced in working with children with cancer and other life-threatening conditions, and approaches this inevitably painful subject delicately yet confidently, using a wealth of short examples of clinical material which vividly illustrate the points she is making. In this slim book Sourkes usefully breaks down the subject into ‘Psychotherapy’, ‘Illness and Treatment’, ‘Impact on Normal Life’, ‘Facets of Awareness’, ‘Anticipatory Grief, and ‘The Dying Child’. There are many line drawings by children and some colour plates. The fact that there is no index is a serious drawback in using the book.

I feel that overall this book is limited by the sparsity of psychoanalytic understanding - the only psychoanalytic author quoted is Winnicott (who is frequently and helpfully used, particularly in understanding play). Thus many of her observations lack depth and insight. For example, Sourkes simplistically writes about the child's relationship with medical caregivers, briefly describing their responses ranging from terror to trust, and concludes with ‘However, most children are eventually able to integrate the staff's caring with the necessary infliction of pain that treatment involves’ (p. 44). Although earlier she explores the possible fantasy of ‘illness as punishment’, her cognitive Piagetian perspective of concrete thinking explains only one aspect of the situation. Her discourse is impoverished by the lack of reference to the realms of unconscious fantasy, the internal and external relationship with the mother/father, previous negotiations of trauma, the resurgence of infantile aggression, persecution, splitting, projection, and so on. Similarly, Sourkes's definition of psychic trauma is a quote from the child psychiatrist, Ten (p. 4). Neither Sourkes nor Terr make reference to Freud's, and later, Anna Freud's formulations on the subject, although in essence the quotation summarizes earlier psychoanalytic formulations. This lack of an academic underpinning, and sometimes lack of depth of understanding, makes the book less stimulating for psychotherapists, but may make it more accessible to the lay reader.

Eight years after his death from a heart attack on a tennis court in the south of France, where stands the reputation of Ronald David Laing, psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, psychotherapist, and let's face it, guru? While much of his work is still available, suggesting a continued interest, I wonder who reads them. Laing's fate in so many fields seems to have been that of marginalization - dismissed as a creature of that poor, maligned decade ‘the sixties’ - when he is not ignored altogether. The psychiatrists, with their continued search for chemical imbalances and organic causes, dismiss his work out of hand; his ideas are ignored by the world of psychoanalysis (even a recent book on the ‘independent mind’ in British psychoanalysis found no place at all for this most independent of minds), while he himself, it is sometimes knowingly muttered, was ‘clearly psychotic’. At the level of popular, dinner party discourse he is constantly misunderstood and misrepresented, his reputation formed by gossip and innuendo, usually from people who never even met him, and general ignorance of what he actually wrote and said. Although profoundly critical of psychiatry, Laing was never, as he kept insisting, an ‘anti-psychiatrist’ or part of the ‘anti-psychiatry’ movement, unlike his one-time colleague David Cooper who coined the term (against Laing's advice, Laing claims). Although fascinated by the workings of the families of people labelled schizophrenic, Laing never ‘blamed’ families or mothers for ‘causing’ the condition. Nor did he think that the ‘mad’ were ‘truly sane’ or the sane mad, although he was fascinated too, obsessed perhaps, by the idea that the discourse of those designated ‘insane’ was, or at least might be, intelligible to anyone prepared to listen without preconceptions.

Laing touched a raw nerve, Kotowicz says at the start of his book. He attempted ‘to politicize and spiritualize, so to speak, the discourse of madness and in the process, in a truly anarchic fashion, he questioned, doubted, ridiculed some of the fundamental precepts that govern our society’ (p. 1). Laing attempted to bring madness back into the public space, where once it had been before it was incarcerated.

Beyond Understanding? Some Thoughts on the Meaning and Function of the Notion of ‘Evil’

Christoph Hering

Christoph Hering

12 Chemin des Eglantiers, 1208 Geneva, Switzerland

Christoph Hering  

The Dream of Dr Lamb's Patient

Dr Lamb whom I supervised in my work abroad had a patient who dreamt the following dream: ‘I am the shepherd of a herd of sheep. I am standing with a bucket full of poisonous food by the fence of the sheep pen. All the sheep of my herd except one are lying on the ground, dead; there is only one sheep left alive and I am about to feed this last sheep with my poisonous food. I imagine with relish how I will be able to witness the slow agony of this last sheep's dying’.

Introduction

We would never think of calling a shark which attacks and kills a swimmer ‘evil’ nor an earthquake which within seconds kills thousands of people.1 ‘Evil’ refers to man and man-made situations. It is a notion which is part of the man-made moral grid of conscience, intention and choice. Whenever I use this term in the paper it appears therefore in inverted commas.

Bad has a counterpart in good, with which it can form a relationship and undergo modification. ‘Evil’, although it may have a counterpart in something like ‘pure angelic innocence’, refers to a situation which is beyond the influence of its counterpart and thus cannot be altered. ‘Evil’ is for my understanding reserved for a kind of unmitigated destructiveness which is absolute.2 It attempts to describe a state of mind in its perpetrator which is totally devoid of any care, concern, guilt, scruple or empathy for the person chosen to be its victim. (A state of mind which, although it is horrific and terrifying, nevertheless exerts great fascination.)3

When I began thinking about what, as a psychoanalyst, I could contribute to the discussion about ‘evil’, I thought that, apart from throwing some light on the very workings of ‘evil’ as I see it, and thus bringing some understanding into what feels so incomprehensible, I would concentrate on a very particular function which I think this term can perform for us. I thought I would try to show how much this notion of ‘evil’ as a realistic threat coming from outside can become and is regularly used as a container for the projection of an internal threat which can feel too frightening and incomprehensible to be available for conscious integration into our self. I would suggest that in this way the notion of ‘evil’ not only serves to name a real threat but also to distance us from the disturbing insight of how much more we ordinary human beings might have in common with the designated perpetrator of it.

Maria Rhode

London

Maria Rhode  

This enormously moving book presents Joanna Fanos's interviews with young adults who had lost a sibling to cystic fibrosis. Her initial concern was that the impact of such a catastrophic loss was little discussed in the professional literature. This professional silence turned out to have many distressing parallels - in the absence of provision geared specifically to the needs of siblings; in the inability of most of the parents to help their surviving children; and, ultimately, in the survivors’ failure to mourn. Not surprisingly, Fanos encountered a high incidence of emotional disturbance and psychosomatic illness; on the hopeful side, the interviews were experienced as therapeutic.

Extensive quotations from Fanos's interviews with the siblings are skilfully woven together so that a composite picture emerges of the immediate and long-term impact of the death. Chapter headings signal the broad themes around which the wealth of material is organized: ‘The family setting’, ‘The sibling relationship’, ‘The sibling's view of the illness’, ‘The ordeal’, ‘The aftermath’, ‘The next year’, ‘Fear’, ‘Waiting’, ‘Guilt’, ‘Resolution’. Statistical methods and results are presented in the Appendix. This mode of presentation works well: quotations tell the reader enough about individual interviewees to convey a feeling of what they were like as human beings and to stimulate the generation of hypotheses.

In 1991, a group of enterprising and enlightened social services professionals banded together to create a new organization called Respond, a unique counselling and psychotherapy service designed to provide treatment for adults struggling with different forms of mental handicap or learning disability. Originally based in Wandsworth, in South London, Respond has now become a pioneering charity, located near Euston Station, staffed with experienced psychodynamically orientated clinicians. The core team at Respond has just published this, its first book, which stands as a very rich and much welcome contribution to the steadily growing literature on the psychotherapy of handicap and disability.

Co-authored by Alan Corbett, the Assistant Director; Tamsin Cottis, Assistant Director; and Stephen Morris, the former Director, the book provides us with a clear, thoughtful and readable primer on this vital, though often neglected, area of practice. The authors describe the development of their working model, based on attachment principles, and discuss the importance of an advocacy-based approach. In brief, this philosophy of advocacy involves the clinician functioning as a witness who believes and validates the abuses which so many patients have suffered, and who then endeavours to provide a setting in which further exploration and mourning can be facilitated. Subsequent chapters focus on more detailed clinical issues, such as the treatment of handicapped patients who abuse substances or who smear bodily products. The authors write with tremendous compassion and humanity, and they illustrate their theoretical postulates with vivid case material.

The professional staff at Respond work with challenging and tragic individuals who not only suffer from organic handicaps, but who have been cruelly victimized by dangerous adults.

From Pain to Violence: The Traumatic Roots of Destructiveness by Felicity de Zulueta. Published by Whurr Publishers, London, 1993; 325 pages: £17.50 paperback.

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache

Lincoln Clinic and Centre for Psychotherapy, London

Robert Tollemache  

Why are people violent? Can psychoanalysis help in answering this question? Dr de Zulueta's work is ground breaking; she establishes plausible links between defects in the process of making attachments and violent behaviour; at the same time she demonstrates wider and more far-reaching connections between object relations theories and mainstream psychology, sociology, ethnography, biochemistry, psychobiology and neurology. One hopes it will receive the widespread attention it deserves. She says that human violence springs from how humans develop, and hence from how they see, and what they feel about, themselves and the ‘other’; that violence is a by-product of psychological trauma. She does not disprove Man's ‘innate’ propensity to violence, but she does draw on suggestive evidence from many different fields of study to support her conclusions to the contrary. Though she is generally immaculately scholarly, her conclusions and the intensity of her accumulated arguments betray her underlying passion.

In outline, she starts from Bowlby's work on attachment, and the deprivation, loss and abuse consequent on the failures of attachment. She notes the effects of trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder, especially in children, on attachment patterns, and connects psychological trauma and child abuse with human destructiveness. Included in this is the compulsion to repeat the trauma, which may be based on an addiction to it. She goes on to describe biochemical patterns which might help to explain why psychological patterns stubbornly resist change. She finishes by reminding us how some cultures sanction adult violence towards children much more than others, and shows how such sanction can be linked with polarized gender roles such that males are perpetrators and women are victims of rape and sexual violence.

This thumb-nail sketch of her original conclusions may whet your appetite, but it cannot convey the range and depth of her thinking, expressed in nearly 300 closely argued pages, drawing on hundreds of references from psychoanalysis, psychology, biochemistry and neurology and ethology. Her scope is so wide ranging and diverse that the trend of her argument is difficult to keep in mind without several readings; so it is essential to summarize its main areas before attempting to consider critically what she has to say.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The theoretical traditions within psychoanalysis are each seen by some adherents as exclusive of the others. Occasionally there are articles that help us to fit the different theories together in a conceptual scheme, bringing them together in a Way that validates each and broadens our understanding of the whole. Our first paper by Bob Hinshelwood is one of these. Hinshelwood places in order three levels of experience: classical symbol-formation, primitive defence mechanisms and the layer beneath them both, the containing function of the body ego as identified by Esther Bick in her notion of the skin as container. Each of these levels has its moment for each individual, but for the analyst to confine himself to one level would amount to reductionism.

In the second paper, containment is also a theme: the early containment by the mother and its relationship to the containment of food in bulimic conditions. Patricia Marsden relates eating disorders to the myth of Demeter and Persephone in which we can see the unresolved struggles of early infancy that are reactivated in the adolescent changes into sexual maturity. Mother and daughter are threatened by both separation and fusion so that Persephone's ritual descent into the underworld and reappearance signify an enactment of primitive oral fears and sexual anxieties simultaneously.

In a third paper about primitive level functioning, Michael Leibowitz introduces a new concept, protective-identification. In the early states of extreme dependency, the infant's terror is of abandonment by its objects. To protect itself from this possible trauma, the infant identifies with its object, through an oral assimilation, creating a narcissistic defence that allows a sense of stability and survival.

Then, the contribution by Sherly Williams addresses the difficulties of the ‘ends and endings’ of therapy: ‘end’ has a dual meaning as both the aims and purposes of therapeutic work as well as the conclusion of a relationship. Williams discusses these aspects and their interconnections.

This is a book written for professionals working with emotionally disturbed children and their families. For those unfamiliar with psychoanalytic concepts it is an introduction to their usefulness and applications. For those who are familiar with psychoanalytic thinking it provides illustrations of ways in which psychoanalytic ideas can be effectively used in a wide variety of community settings which deal with children and their families, such as hospital departments, community health and family centres and schools. Contributors to the book are drawn from child and adult psychoanalytic psychotherapy, psychiatry, social work, psychology, teaching and other related fields. The book thus reflects the multidisciplinary collaboration it advocates, although it is also evident that the contributors have a shared grounding in psychoanalytic thought and practice. The individual chapters are, in a sense, personal testimony to their writers' innovative work in settings that were often not geared to sensitive response to troubled young minds.

The editors place these innovative projects in the broad socio-political framework of society today: social and economic trends, legislation, and the changes in service provision as a result of the introduction of the concept of an internal market in health, education and welfare. In describing the ‘external world’ of many children subject to poverty and deprivation, the authors emphasize the links between social and economic factors and child mental health.

Judy Cooper

Judy Cooper

London

Judy Cooper  

This book fills a gap in the literature. What Laplanche and Pontalis have done for Freud, and Hinshelwood for Klein, has now been rendered by Jan Abram for Winnicott, undoubtedly one of the greats of modern day psychoanalysis.

Winnicott was a prolific and popular writer and was able to convey intricate psychoanalytic ideas not just to psychoanalysts but to readers in neighbouring disciplines and lay audiences. Some professionals have described his books as ‘a jolly read’ although, looking at his writing more closely, one can appreciate how dense and convoluted his theories are. Winnicott seemed not to be a systematic theoretician and never wrote in detail about his therapeutic approach, so it could appear random. Abram's dictionary, by giving definitions, explanations, quotations and references, demonstrates how his theories are quite systematic, being firmly grounded in therapeutic principles, and how he has attempted to widen the scope of psychoanalysis. She organizes Winnicott's main ideas under 22 headings, including many concepts which do not ordinarily get much attention paid to them.

David Riley

David Riley

London

David Riley  

Quem Jupiter vult perdere dementat prius.

(Whom God would destroy, he first sends mad.)

The name of R.D. Laing will be familiar to all readers of this Journal though there may be variable knowledge of the content of his work. This is a compelling biography which describes the man and the work and attempts to trace some of the links between the two. It does not attempt a critique of Laing's theoretical contribution, though questions about that are naturally bound to arise. Indeed, this could be a study of one of those exceptional people who achieve guru status in their own lifetime. One consequence of this is that a merger occurs between the person and their work which is at first enjoyed, but eventually suffered, as one sees in the lives of many of our twentieth-century public figures, especially those of a charismatic type.

This biography could be read from many angles: for example, it might be a case study of such a merger and could demonstrate that, when this occurs, the ideas increasingly cannot be heard because of the noise and seduction generated by charisma. When ideas cannot be heard, development cannot take place. A form of leadership which is anti-development triumphs, the very opposite of a psychoanalytic attitude.

A cautionary note before conveying some of the spirit of the book. The dust-jacket refers to the man who ‘became Britain's most famous psychoanalyst’. This seems both misleading and mischievous. It is misleading because, although Laing qualified as a psychoanalyst-contentiously, as Clay clearly documents, because he was so contemptuous of the training organization, he was even then becoming estranged from it. In The Divided Self-written before the age of 30-he avows his debt more to existential philosophy than to psychoanalysis. This theoretical stance was soon to be put into practice in a characteristically uncompromising manner with the foundation of Kingsley Hall. This existential emphasis also ran in tandem with clinical practices, for example, taking LSD with patients, which most psychoanalysts would eschew. The mischievous aspect is that the inevitable impression building up throughout the book is of a man sucked into a destructive vortex which directly, or by association, affects all those in his ambit. This, of course, includes the two professions which contributed considerably to his status-medicine and psychoanalysis.

Psychotherapy Research6(4): 223-47, 1996

Clients' Perceptions of Treatment for Depression: I. Helpful Aspects

John J. Gershefski, Diane B. Arnkoff, Carol R. Glass and Irene Elkin

Clients' perspectives on the helpful aspects of treatment were examined using post-treatment data from the NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program. Averaged across treatments, perceptions that were coded as indicative of common aspects of the treatments, such as the helpfulness of the therapist, were reported most frequently. There were no group differences; thus, in the placebo plus clinical management group, responses were coded into common-factor categories no less often than in the other groups. However, cognitive-behaviour therapy clients and imipramine plus clinical management clients gave responses coded as reflecting aspects that were specific to the treatment they received significantly more often than did clients in the other conditions.



Psychotherapy Research6(4): 249-62,1996

Clients' Perceptions of Treatment for Depression: II. Problematic or Hindering Aspects

James A. Levy, Carol R. Glass, Diane B. Arnkoff, John J. Gershefskiirene Elkin

Clients’ perceptions of the problematic or hindering aspects of treatment in the NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program were investigated, from the perspective of factors hypothesized to be common across treatments and those hypothesized to be specific to one type of treatment. Overall, 36% of the 154 treatment completers indicated that something was problematic for them about their treatment or about their participation in the research. It was primarily clients in the imipramine plus clinical management and placebo plus clinical management conditions who gave responses categorized as specific to the treatment they had received, which for imipramine clients consisted primarily of complaints related to medication side effects. In addition, a small subset of pharmacotherapy clients indicated that they wanted psychotherapy. There were no significant differences among treatment conditions in the report of problems categorized as aspects common across all the treatments, such as therapist techniques and personal qualities. However, the report of a problem coded as a common aspect identified a small group of clients (n = 15) whose treatment outcome was comparatively less favourable.

[[RunningHead]]

Demonology versus Science?

Felicity de Zulueta B.Sc MA Cantab M.B.Ch.B. M.R.C. Psych

Felicity de Zulueta

Denmark Hill, London SE5 8AZ

Felicity de Zulueta  

I would like to begin my talk today by asking you all a question: were you drawn here by the title of this conference or did you come despite its title? I ask you this because I had difficulties with the title of today's gathering. Was I to just ignore it and speak about the traumatic origins of violence, or was I to address my discomfort and that of some of my colleagues who were surprised to see my name associated with the subject of ‘evil’? I have decided to try and make sense of being invited to a cathedral and a talk on ‘evil’ by thoughtful people who are as concerned as I am in addressing the issue of human violence.

You may well ask why am I making such a fuss about this business of ‘evil’? What does it evoke to you? For me, brought up as a Catholic, the concept of ‘evil’ is linked to the devil, to Satan, to the punishment of hell, to sin and demonology. It allows those who use such concepts to feel morally superior and good whilst those who are branded ‘evil’ are seen as bad and inhuman. There is no need to understand evil but there is a need to deal with it through punishment. Our society has a long history of labelling its deviants as ‘evil’ and then dealing with them through imprisonment, torture, murder and even genocide. The moral labelling of our violent members of society as ‘evil’ does not help us learn about the causes of violence and can in fact inhibit any serious attempts to understand or prevent it. If we dehumanize those who carry out terrible acts of cruelty, we can forget that they were probably once human beings like you and me and we lose any interest in trying to find out what made them into the ‘monsters’ they now appear.

However, I will acknowledge that what we seem to lack is a word that truly describes the horror, the terror and the pain of those who are on the receiving end of such people. A woman who was raped repeatedly by her father as a child and then subjected as an adult to the most horrific experiences at the hands of a man who tortured her in all possible ways asked me: ‘How can I convey what he is to me without using the word “evil”? There is no other word that communicates some of what I feel’. And I agree that we are short of such a word and that it conveys something of the subjective experience of being totally violated.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Concerning Signs and Symbols

Donald Meltzer

Donald Meltzer

23 Alexandra Road, Oxford OX2 0DD

Donald Meltzer  

The paper I wrote in 1971, ‘On Sincerity’, was inspired by reading Wittgenstein's work in linguistic philosophy. In his Philosophical Investigations Wittgenstein (1953) spends quite a long time discussing meaning, the difference between ‘saying it’ and ‘meaning it’. This drew my attention to the problem in analysis, both the analyst's problem in meaning what he says to his patient, and the problem for the patient in meaning the things he says to the analyst. In the course of investigating this I became aware that language is not a very disciplined way of ‘meaning it’ because language is so conventional. This led me on to a clearer differentiation in linguistic structures between signs and symbols, which tend to be equated with one another in works of people like de Saussure and Lacan. The thing about signs is that they are just a way of pointing at things, using words to point. They consist almost exclusively of the conventional naming of things and functions. Now, in so far as people use signs in communicating with one another, they cannot ‘mean it’ because they cannot mean anything, they are simply pointing at the world. Symbols are entirely different and very mysterious, because they are utterly intuitive and are containers for emotional meaning. One would be inclined to say, in so far as people use symbols in communicating with one another, they automatically ‘mean it’.

But a difficulty arises because not all symbols are autonomous, that is, created in the mind of the speaker. Most of the symbols we use in our communication are conventional, received symbols, which we have received from other people. They are like the currency we use in our daily life. They become worn out currency. In so far as one utilizes these worn out received symbols it is very difficult to convey emotional meaning. A received symbol is like an old coin in which you can make out the head, but not any features of the monarch. Another difficulty about using received symbols to convey emotion is that the emotions that they convey are only the shadows of emotion, the background of emotion, and contain very little that is particular or passionate. To convey emotional meaning by language is not just a matter of symbol, not just a matter of words; it is also a matter of the music. It's a very striking thing that when you hear poets reading their own poetry it is very peculiar music they make. They seem to drone. I'm thinking of T.S. Eliot, and the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas. They drone a kind of incantation. It is the opinion of Suzanne Langer that the origin of symbol formation, palaeontologically speaking, is in chanting, the music of chanting and dance. The rhythms of primitive dance. So it's not surprising or unintelligible that, when you hear poets reading their own poetry, they chant it, and one would also think that they might wish to be stamping their feet, like flamenco dancers.

‘Too Early, Too Late?’: Endings in Psychotherapy - An Attachment Perspective

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Barnstaple, Devon EX31 4JB

Jeremy Holmes  

Endings in psychoanalytic psychotherapy are often problematic, especially in publicly-funded therapies. Endings may be premature or delayed - ‘too soon’ or ‘too late’. This paper looks at some parallels between endings in literature and endings in psychotherapy; considers the gender bias in Freud's ‘Analysis Terminable and Interminable’; introduces evidence from psychotherapy research; and puts forward an attachment-informed approach to ending, based on the distinction between avoidant and ambivalent attachment and how this may be played out by both therapist and patient in the transference-countertransfence matrix. A controlling therapist with an avoidant patient may end ‘too early’, an over-empathic therapist with an ambivalent patient may end ‘too late’. Clinical examples illustrate these theoretical points.

Men Who Leave Too Soon: Reflections on the Erotic Transference and Countertransference1

Joy Schaverien PHD

Joy Schaverien

1 The Square, South Luffenham, Oakham, Leics LEI 5 8NS

Joy Schaverien  

It is observed that certain male patients, in psychotherapy with female therapists, end prematurely. Attention to common factors in the cases of the ‘men who leave too soon’ reveals a pattern. Some leave to avoid intimacy, others to avoid consciousness of erotic/aggressive impulses where the feminine may be alternately idealized and denigrated in the transference. Unconscious collusion in traditional gender dynamics may contribute to avoidance of consciousness of sexual feelings in the countertransference. This may sometimes result in interpretation of eros in infantile terms in denial of the adult, sexual dynamic. Vignettes from clinical practice illustrate the theoretical discussion.

The Generation of Psychoanalytic Knowledge: Sociological and Clinical Perspectives Part One: ‘Give Me a Consulting Room …’1

Michael Rustin

Michael Rustin

Longbridge Road, Dagenham RM8 2AS

Michael Rustin  

This paper examines the contradiction between the advances of psychoanalysis over the near century since Freud invented it, and its apparent divergence from the procedures of the other sciences. It argues that developments in the sociology and history of science since the 1960s enable the different dimensions of scientific activity to be more objectively identified. The work of Bruno Latour is discussed, focusing on his account of the laboratory as the key site of scientific discovery, and leading to a comparison between the laboratory and the psychoanalytic consulting room. However, significant differences between laboratory-based science and psychoanalysis are also pointed out. The most important of these is the degree to which the control of the outside world routinely sought by normal sciences is made impossible and undesirable for psychoanalysis by its distinctive commitment to the autonomy of its human subjects.

Paul Holmes

Paul Holmes

Paul Holmes  

Drama might be said to be a key to life. It certainly may be a central aspect in many forms of psychotherapy; for example, Salvador Minuchin (Minuchin & Fishman 1981) has described the importance of the drama of enactment in family therapy whilst Joyce McDougall (1986) has addressed the same issue from a classical psychoanalytic perspective in her book Theatres of the Mind. Illusions and Truth on the Psychoanalytic Stage. This said I suspect that, for many psychotherapists, the involvement of drama in the therapeutic process is more often associated in their minds with ‘acting out’ (which may threaten or destroy the work with their patients) than with any appropriate therapeutic activity.

These five books, in their different ways, give elegant reasons why drama, in the context of dramatherapy (and, in the case of Chris Farmer's contribution, psychodrama) must be given its proper position within the broad family of the psychotherapies practised in this country. The UK Council for Psychotherapy has long recognized psychodrama as a respectable form of psychotherapy. Now the dramatherapists too are deeply involved in the negotiations which, they hope, will see their professional association become a member of the UKCP. There are, however, significant differences between these books and each will meet different needs in their readers. The two edited volumes on specific themes (work with children and brief therapy) show all the variability in style typical of such collections of chapters. However, both will make rewarding reading for any psychotherapist with a particular interest in these very important topics.

The other three books reflect the work of single authors. Robert Landy's volume is a collection of his papers published over a 13 year time span. Phil Jones and Chris Farmer, on the other hand, attempt in their books to bring together their professional experiences gained over several years in as focused and coherent a manner as possible. Thus each book in this collection provides the reader with a different slant and opportunity to discover more about what these dramatic therapies may be able to offer those in need of therapeutic help with their emotional worlds. All I can now attempt to do in this brief review is to give a flavour of each book.

Protective-Identification: A Narcissistic Defence against Primary Object Loss

Michael Leibowitz

Michael Leibowitz

3 Elbridge Farm Cottages, Sturry, Canterbury, Kent CT3 4AU

Michael Leibowitz  

In this paper, the writer introduces the theoretical concept of Protective-Identification as a defence mechanism. As an ego adaptive strategy, Protective-Identification allows the ego to remain defensively attached to internal objects. As a form of protection against trauma or feared loss or abandonment by the object, the infantile ego resorts to oral assimilation defences in order to preserve harmonious internal ego-object relations and ego-object cathexes. It is argued here that Protective-Identification as a defence operates at the regressed level of primary narcissistic identification with the object at the cost of integrated ego autonomy.

Bion: A Freudian Innovator

Parthenope Bion Talamo

Parthenope Bion Talamo

Via G. La Pira 9, 10093, Collegno, Torino, Italy

Parthenope Bion Talamo  

There is one remarkably short paper by W.R. Bion which constitutes a sort of crossroads or nodal point for the understanding of many aspects of his work in general. In ‘Notes on Memory and Desire’1 he describes something, a point of technique, which is at the same time very Freudian and yet can also be seen to link up to a series of theories that make Bion seem to be one of the least Freudian of psychoanalysts. I intend to take this paper as my reference point and use it to show how Bion both continued faithfully within the main lines of Freud's thought and was also an original thinker.

Historically speaking, the question as to whether Bion was a Freudian or not has never arisen, because he was thought of as being a Kleinian, and since Klein had, though with some controversy, been cleared of the charge of being unfaithful to psychoanalytic theory, it would seem that her followers, or those who were thought to be such, were also automatically accepted as being bona fide psychoanalysts. Over the years, people have asked me questions about the ‘background’ which shows through every now and again in Bion's writings; the questions can be said to range from ‘Was he interested in aesthetics?’ to ‘Did he read Zen Buddhism?’ passing through logic, mathematics, philosophy and a great many other subjects too. Rarely, or perhaps never, have I been asked whether Bion read Freud, since I suppose that it is taken for granted that he did; and yet the ways in which Freud's thinking permeated Bion's, and the degree to which it did so, are neither so obvious nor so automatic - there is not too much ‘of course’ about it.

Freud's own requirements for those who professed to call themselves psychoanalysts were quite simply and succinctly stated: conviction in the existence of the unconscious and use of the transference as the primary therapeutic instrument. Bion certainly did not depart from these basic theories and, indeed, he is a great deal more faithful to many other Freudian theories and ways of thinking than the important use which he makes of Klein's concept of projective identification might make him appear.

This paper discusses the under-used ideas of Esther Bick.
