Donald Meltzer  

First of all, that's [Parthenope Bion Talamo's paper] what I call a hard act to follow - the word from the castle making us all feel peasants down in the courtyard. What I want to speak about is first of all to tell you my thoughts on material from observation and clinical analysis. Then I want to talk about what - you might say pretentiously - I would call the sociology of genius, the situation which Bion himself has written about, and the position of the genius in the group, and with some ideas about the internal life of the genius as well.

To start with some material, just to give you something in the back of your mind that has to do with what has been called the origin of object relations - and is really the origin of confusion about objects. There are three bits of material. Two of them are from seminars in Venice.

The first was an observation of a child and her mother - an 18-month-old child who was living with a mother whose husband had deserted her. The two of them were in a rather bad state of absolute adhesiveness to one another that prevented both of them from eating and they were getting emaciated. A very, I think, talented social worker was called in who functioned simply as an observer, hardly saying a word but tolerating the clingingness of both child and mother, observing their interaction and trying to understand it. Over a period of six months the introduction of a third person into this adhesive relationship significantly altered things so that both child and mother began to manifest mental processes and not simply this adhesiveness that seemed to be devoid of phantasy and devoid of emotions. And their feeding improved as well. The child began to play, began to exhibit naughtiness. The mother began to have emotions towards the child and so on. It seemed to be accomplished simply by being there as an interested and thoughtful observer, observing this adhesiveness and its mindlessness.

The second piece of material from the same seminar was a report of a preliminary interview with a seven-and-a-half-year-old boy who was thought to be autistic, who was unable to speak. But he wasn't terribly troublesome or manifesting great disturbance - he just seemed to be ineducable. During an hour's interview he didn't play. The interviewer tried to interest him in various things and the boy seemed to get irritable towards him. Then, touching upon his experience at school, he asked the boy whether they did any music at school. The boy brightened up and said ‘Yes’, and went to the blackboard and drew what strongly resembled a stave of notes of music. He couldn't sing it but the pictorial representation of it seemed to please him.

Introduction

The title of this paper was suggested to me when my patient, Chris, told me about a television film by Dennis Potter. The film, Secret Friends, which reflected Chris's own preoccupations, was about a married man who lived a fairly respectable life on the surface but who had a darker side, a secret life both in fantasy and in reality where he explored the underworld.

Chris and I have also explored her own personal underworld where we have met many characters: an evil witch, a perverted old man, a prostitute and a young boy (among others). As we have got to know these inner figures we have come to see them, despite her negative associations, not only as enemies but also as friends, the secret friends who have helped us with Chris's individuation process, her path to wholeness, integration and a deeper understanding of who she is and whom she might become.

In this paper I also consider the process of working with patients who have a history of sexual abuse and who, from a diagnostic perspective, are often classified as borderline personalities. In particular, I focus upon the parallels and discrepancies between borderline symptomatology, familiar to analysts, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which perhaps receives less attention. I think that an interplay between the two approaches in the mind of the analyst helps to illuminate an understanding of the transference/countertransference constellation.

Background

Chris is a petite, attractive woman of 33. She is the second youngest of five, in a lowermiddle-class Catholic family. She is a senior lecturer. When Chris was 7 her father had a major heart attack and her mother then had to return to work.

Chris's presenting symptoms were of depression and suicidal thoughts following the break-up of her relationship with Tom, her boyfriend of the past 10 years. She had been seeing a counsellor twice weekly for the previous year. As her depression deepened, her counsellor referred her to the British Association of Psychotherapists and her GP prescribed her anti-depressants and referred her to the local psychiatric hospital, where she was seen daily in the emergency clinic.

Treatment with the patient described here, a 28-year-old man in a Regional Secure Unit on a Pre-Discharge ward who had murdered his mother during late adolescence, was aimed at altering the intrapsychic factors through transference-based psychoanalytical psychotherapy in order to facilitate a change of attachment to the internal mother/object and to women, whom he had devalued at part-object level, based on his primitive perception of his mother as ‘Satan's dog’ and the ‘devil's jackal’. Some of Bion'S Ideas on Meaning and Understanding

David Taylor

David Taylor

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

David Taylor  

Bion described his four books, Learning From Experience (1962), Elements of Psychoanalysis (1963), Transformations (1965), and Attention and Interpretation (1970), as setting out a theory of psychoanalytic observation rather than psychoanalysis as such. This is similar to the way in which a philosopher of science tries to understand scientific method rather than being concerned directly with specific items of scientific knowledge. The philosopher of science uses particular experiments to illustrate the principles underlying scientific experiments, and in those four books that was Bion's method. His clinical examples were very schematic abstracts intended as reminders to an experienced readership.

However, Bion's claim that he was not writing psychoanalysis was a little disingenuous. Many people have found Bion's illustrative observations of great value in their own right. In these illustrations he formulated clinical problems and phenomena, to use Bion's term ‘configurations’, which illuminate previously undescribed aspects of the personality. This work of Bion's also contains the basis of a psychoanalytic theory of meaning and understanding and this is the subject of this paper. I hope to show how these ideas can be helpful in clinical work with patients as well having general and theoretical interest. Of course, meaning and understanding are big subjects and the, therefore, incomplete theory of meaning that I will be describing will not touch on, for instance, philosophical or psycholinguistic aspects.

I am taking a psychoanalytic theory of meaning and understanding to refer to the consideration of the role of emotional factors, especially infantile and primitive ones, in the development of meaning. By meaning I am intending two approximate, general senses. The first is that of general significance - how much, or how little, someone or something means to us. An example of this would be the phrase, ‘life has a great deal of meaning’. The second is the way in which systems of representation, be they language or pictures, can operate as carriers of information and in the specific context of this paper as vehicles of information about human experience. The various forms of that experience can have important effects upon these systems of representation. By the term understanding two things are intended. One is the emotional process where one person comes to understand another, and the second the process internal to an individual of ‘understanding’, of discovering meaning.

Ivan Ward

Ivan Ward

20 Maresfield Gardens, London NW3 5SX

Ivan Ward  

Dear Sami Timimi

I thought I would write a letter because, paradoxically, what I have to say is not ‘personal’. It is just that your paper (BJP 13(2): 183-92, 1997) was the latest in a long line of psychoanalytic examinations of racism which I believe are simply wrong, and I would like to tell you why. The Kleinian approach you follow, involving the ‘splitting and projection’ or ‘paranoid-schizoid’ model, is now the dominant form in which racism is understood. Unfortunately, the prevalence of this view has had the effect of inhibiting rather than facilitating thinking about the problem. Neither does it account for the facts.

Of course you must be aware of this in practice. When dealing with the cited case material you bring in a wealth of oedipal and other factors which the paranoidschizoid model misses. The case material breaks the bounds of the theoretical framework with which you open your paper. So why cling to the theory?

I think we would both agree that racism must be a complicated and composite structure with different aspects. Otherwise what's the point of analysis - which consists of taking things apart? Each of these aspects are themselves complex structures. The way in which other people ‘disappear’ from view and their humanity is lost sight of. How does it happen; what mechanisms are involved? The way imaginary fears are conjured up and seem to be real - for instance, the phantasy of being raped by a black man, or the idea of threats to the ‘purity of blood’. Where do the fears come from, and how do they achieve their sense of reality? The way we blame other people - seek someone to blame - and the connection to feelings of humiliation or guilt we may be trying to expunge. In what contexts does this become socially acceptable and generalized? The process of altering reality in order to preserve a feature that seems to be essential to our psychical well-being, as the racist may preserve illusions about his own history or cultural heroes; what are the anxieties that motivate such a manoeuvre? What we call racism involves all of these features and more. It is a composite structure which cannot be reduced to formulaic description, but rather should be taken apart, analysed, slowly piece by piece.

Darren Wolf

14 Pendrell House, New Compton Street, London WC2H 8DF

Darren Wolf  

This paper examines how homosexuality has been described by a number of writers on the subject, and compares these accounts with the author's experience of his own sexuality. A critique is offered of contemporary accounts of homosexuality on grounds of their inconsistency and inadequacy: this is illustrated with specific examples of sexual behaviour from research findings and the press. Clinical material shows clients' sexual experiences are as varied and diverse as the multiplicity of theoretical accounts which seek to explain them. The importance of caution on the part of the psychotherapist when making sense of sexual material is emphasized.

[The material was sent to the three commentators, asking them to take up areas that interested them about the content of the session or the technique of the therapist. - KA]

The Patient

Mrs A is a 47-year-old white woman who is divorced, lives alone and has a weekend partner and a challenging job in senior management. She came for psychotherapy when her defences against unbearable anxiety broke down. She had been prescribed Prozac and sleeping pills by her GP which she felt had not helped. She was unable to rest day or night and could no longer go to work. An earlier psychotherapy seven years previously, which lasted for five years, had helped. She wanted a different therapist this time. The previous therapy, she said, helped her to come to terms with not being able to have a child with her then husband, from whom she was finally divorced the previous year after a few years' separation.

Her most important anxiety was that she would go mad like her mother did when she was a child and there was an unspoken fear that she might, like mother, kill herself. At the initial consultation she reported missing the close friendship she had with a woman friend and colleague with whom she had lived in between her marriage ending (husband left) and starting the new relationship she was now in for two years. She felt insufficiently supported by her partner. It emerged that he was wanting them to live together. She thought she could not cope with a job and a partner. In passing, Mrs A told me that she had a hysterectomy' during the previous year and that ‘it was clean - there was no cut’ and that she had made an excellent recovery.

She presented as feeling thoroughly persecuted by bad internal objects. Her place of work, which was previously a safe space where she felt important, became a polluted space in which her identity was disturbed. She felt herself to be incompetent and useless professionally and very frightened of having her worst fears confirmed by a coming government inspection. She placed herself in a high profile role in between the institution and the inspectors - which spoke highly of her oedipal position - and had then felt terrified of being found wanting. A proposed sacking of a black male colleague whom she ‘adopted’ into her institution in an idealization of ‘minority ethnic’ people seemed to cause her a particularly strong anxiety. It seemed that in her mind the threatened sacking was linked with a threat of sacking (of father by his employers and of mother by her husband) which was the trigger to her family tragedy. I now wish to turn to the diagnosis I made. It seemed that losing her mother at a young age, and by suicide, before she had established a good mother inside of her was of the greatest importance. It was evident that she had tried various strategies for coping with what was undoubtedly a tragedy. One of these was finding mother substitutes - the loss of the latest one was part of the presenting problem.

Commentary by a Lacanian Psychoanalyst

Darian Leader

Darian Leader

10 Upper Wimpole Street, London W1M 7TD

Darian Leader  

The case discussed is a fragment of a psychotherapy. Although the aims of a psychotherapy may be different from those of an analysis, in terms of responding to a situation of suffering, certain connections between material offered by the patient will be necessary to obtain anything more than short-term relief. In this brief comment on the case, I will try to show how the perspectives of Lacanian psychoanalysis may shed light on such connections and the framework in which they are structured.

In the early stages of a treatment, most clinicians would agree on the importance of establishing some of the central coordinates of the family history, although many crucial details will emerge, of course, much later on. The format of a short clinical presentation obviously makes such a historical sketch limited, but one would nonetheless like to know more about the start of the earlier period of therapy and its termination, about the details of the mother's swallowing of tablets (their name) and about the course of the patient's childhood. When the grandfather is described as cruel, for example, one would like further associations here. Now, in terms of the family history that is available in the commentary, there are clues as to the difficulties that are faced by the patient, which revolve around ‘not being able to cope’ with both her job and her partner. This disjunction between job and partner may have significant resonances, in terms of the father's own dilemma of a choice, as it were, between his career and his wife. The wife had indeed swallowed the pills at the time when the father considers returning abroad for his work. This disjunction of work and partner has many echoes in the material (for example, the sacking of the colleagues), and it may not be unconnected to the moments when she was led to enter therapy.

W. Clifford M. Scott (1903-1997)

Athol Hughes

Athol Hughes

Athol Hughes  

Clifford Scott, whose death in January 1997 brought to an end almost seven decades of dedication to psychoanalysis, was a pioneer in many senses. He was one of the first to use psychoanalysis to treat schizophrenic and manic-depressive patients; he was probably the most intensely interested analyst in the psychodynamics of sleeping and dreaming and areas between (Scott 1975); he had a remarkable empathy for, and contact with, the infantile mind, and was dedicated to the development of child analysis in Canada, long before child analysis was generally accepted in analytic trainings in North America. He thought there was no better way to gain contact with our own inner world than through the analysis of a young child.

Clifford Scott was born in 1903 in a small Ontario town. His studies of medicine at the University of Toronto were followed by psychiatric training in New York, Baltimore and Boston. In the latter centres he met many analysts and became interested in pursuing an analytic career. He was encouraged to come to England and did so in 1931. He started adult and child psychoanalytic training in the British PsychoAnalytical Society and was Melanie Klein's first candidate to quality as a psychoanalyst in 1933. He worked at the Maudsley and the Cassel Hospitals until the start of the Second World War when he served in various centres as an Emergency Medical Service psychiatrist. After the war he continued his hospital work and started private practice in London.

He held many important posts in the British Psycho-Analytical Society and was elected President in 1953. His term of office was cut short when he decided to accept a post as Associate Professor in the Department of Psychiatry of McGill University in 1954. He then became one of the founding members of the Canadian Psychoanalytic Society and was influential in the development of a training organization for psychoanalysis in Canada. Over the years, thanks to a large extent to Clifford Scott's efforts, training of analysts not only flourished in French and English-speaking institutes in Montreal but also in Toronto and Ottawa.
